description: The Argus C4 is a 35mm fixed-lens rangefinder introduced in 1951, selling over 300,000 units as Argus’s modernized follow-up to the C3. It features a coupled coincident-image rangefinder integrated into a bright eye-level viewfinder and a permanently mounted 50mm f/2.8 Cintar lens with 10-blade aperture. The camera uses a behind-the-lens leaf shutter offering speeds from 1/10 to 1/300 s (early models to 1/200) and includes a hot shoe with evolving sync options across versions. Several iterations exist, most notably a rare all-black variant with no serial number and believed to be a very limited prototype run. The C4’s popularity eventually led to the Geiss-modified interchangeable-lens C4 and later the dedicated Argus C44 system.

The Bronica EC, released in 1972, was a 6x6 medium format SLR that replaced the S2A and introduced electronic focal plane shutter control to Bronica's lineup. Initially bundled with 75mm Nikkor lenses, production issues led Bronica to switch to their own 80mm f/2.8 MC Zenzanon lenses manufactured by Carl Zeiss Jena. The camera featured a redesigned split mirror system with incompatible film backs and viewfinders compared to previous models, though it maintained lens compatibility. The EC-TL variant (1975) became one of the first 6x6 SLRs to offer built-in TTL metering with aperture priority mode, while the later EC-TL-II revision simplified electronics but removed slow shutter speeds and manual metering capability. This series represented Bronica's final focal plane 6x6 design before transitioning to the leaf-shutter SQ series in 1980.

The Bronica ETR is a medium format rangefinder released in 1976. It is known for its leaf shutter based camera system. The ETR lens system has a Seiko manufactured electronic shutter with speed of 8 sec. to 1/500 sec. Since it's a leaf shutter based camera, flash sync is available at all speeds. Changeable holders make the system more flexible compared to the original M645

The Bronica ETRS is an improved version of the ETR. The main improvement is the interchangeable viewfinder system. The newer AE II and III finders are not fully compatible with the older ETR cameras, because there is a new electronic connector pin. The shutter button lock has been redesigned. It has three settings, unlocked, shutter release button lock but drive and cable release unlocked, and all locked. The neck strap mount has been changed to a design with an eyelet while the previous one was a spring catch style mount used on the Bronica 6x6's

The Bronica GS-1, introduced in March 1983, was Bronica's largest 6x7 format SLR and the first medium format camera with TTL flash metering capability. The modular system featured electronic Seiko #0 leaf shutters in all lenses, allowing flash synchronization at all speeds, with a complete PG lens lineup from 50mm to 500mm focal lengths. Its design prioritized portability over the competing heavy Mamiya RZ/RB systems by rejecting rotating backs, though this meant accepting smaller maximum apertures due to the #0 shutter limitations. The camera offered multiple viewfinder options including a unique rotary AE-prism for vertical shooting, and supported various film formats (6x4.5, 6x6, 6x7, Polaroid) through interchangeable backs. Production ended in June 2002 with approximately 22,500 bodies manufactured, making it a relatively rare professional medium format system.

The Bronica RF645 is a medium format rangefinder camera that was introduced in 2000. It is known for its compact and lightweight design, making it a popular choice among photographers who want a portable medium format camera. The RF645 features a fixed lens with a focal length of 65mm, which is equivalent to a 35mm lens on a full-frame camera. It has a built-in light meter for easy exposure control and offers both manual and aperture priority modes. The camera uses 120 and 220 roll film, allowing for 15 or 30 exposures respectively. It has a bright and clear viewfinder with a rangefinder focusing system, making it easy to achieve accurate focus. The RF645 is a reliable and versatile camera that is well-suited for street photography, travel, and landscape photography.

The Bronica SQ-A is a medium format film camera that was introduced in 1980. It is part of the Bronica SQ series, which was known for its modular design and high-quality lenses. The SQ-A features a waist-level viewfinder and a square 6x6cm format. It has a robust build with a metal body and a reliable mechanical shutter. The camera offers interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to choose from a wide range of focal lengths. It has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure readings and a mirror lock-up function for reducing camera shake. The SQ-A is a versatile camera suitable for both studio and outdoor photography.

The Bronica S2, released in 1965, was a 6x6 focal plane SLR that succeeded the Bronica S and introduced a key innovation: a removable helical focusing mount that could accommodate lenses from 40mm to 200mm. The camera featured a vertical-traveling cloth focal plane shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/1000s, supported both 120 and 220 roll film through an improved film back design, and operated entirely mechanically without requiring batteries. The S2A revision in 1969 maintained identical specifications but improved the film advance gear mechanism to reduce jamming issues and featured a smaller advance dial. Both models were typically bundled with the 75mm f/2.8 Nikkor P lens and offered chrome or black finishes, continuing production until 1977 when they were superseded by the electronic Bronica EC series.

The Bronica ETRSi is an improved version of the ETRS, based on its second revision. It features a mirror lockup switch, TTL flash metering with an OTF flash exposure feature, and a red indicator in the viewfinder when multiple exposure mode is enabled. A traditional bulb mode shutter setting is available, though it consumes power. The film advance gearing mechanism has been improved, and the lower half of the body has enhanced grip areas. The lens release has been moved back to the front of the camera, and the film back holder EI has an improved locking dark slide system.

The Bronica SQ-Ai is a 6x6 medium format SLR camera, announced at the 1990 Photokina and available in the US from early 1991. It is an updated version of the SQ-A, featuring the ability to use a motor drive specifically designed for the Ai model. The camera also supports OTF metering and TTL automatic flash with SCA flash adapters. It includes a longer shutter speed of 16 seconds and a traditional bulb mode, though these do not work with ME or MF finders. The SQ-Ai uses 4x LR44 batteries for power. Production of this model, along with its lenses and accessories, ceased in September 2003.

The Bronica S2A, released in 1969, is a medium format SLR and the successor to the S2. It shares nearly identical specifications and outer appearance with the S2. The primary difference is an improved film advance gear mechanism, which is known to reduce jams. Additionally, the film advance and cocking dial on the S2A is smaller than that of its predecessor. Early S2A models can be identified by "S2A" appearing after the serial number, while later models produced after 1973 (after serial number 150037) lack this designation and feature wingless camera strap lugs.

The Bronica SQ series is a line of 6x6 medium format SLR camera systems, introduced in 1980, with production of the last SQ-Ai model concluding in September 2003. The Bronica SQ, released in August 1980, replaced the Bronica EC as their 6x6 format camera. Similar to the earlier 6x4.5 ETR series, the SQ uses a leaf shutter based lens design, which is not compatible with older focal plane shutter cameras. Its lens system features a Seiko-manufactured electronic shutter with speeds from 8 seconds to 1/500 second, plus T mode, and includes a focusing helicoid built into each lens. A key feature of this leaf shutter system is flash synchronization at all speeds. The camera also incorporates an interchangeable back system that can use 120 or 220 film, with ISO speed dials on the backs that couple with metered finders. The SQ-A, released in 1982, added mirror lockup and a new viewfinder system supporting auto exposure. The SQ-Am, introduced in January 1983, was an integrated motor-drive-only version of the SQ-A. The SQ-Ai, announced at Photokina 1990, was an updated SQ-A with motor drive capability, OTF metering, and TTL automatic flash support. The SQ-B, made in 1996, is a simplified version of the SQ-A.

The Canon A-1 is a popular 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Canon in 1978. It is part of Canon's A-series of cameras and is known for its advanced features and versatility. The A-1 features a fully automatic program mode, as well as aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual exposure modes, giving photographers a wide range of creative control. It has a durable and well-built body, with a comfortable grip and intuitive controls. The A-1 also has a bright and clear viewfinder, allowing for easy framing and focusing. It uses Canon's FD lens mount, which offers a wide selection of high-quality lenses to choose from. Overall, the Canon A-1 is a reliable and capable camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Canon AE-1 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Canon in 1976. Its name refers to the fact that it's an electronic camera using the aperture for automatic exposure (shutter speed priority). It uses an electronically controlled, electromagnet horizontal cloth focal plane shutter, with a speed range of 2 to 1/1000 second plus Bulb and flash X-sync of 1/60 second. The AE-1 was the vanguard of the landmark Canon amateur level A-series SLRs and led Canon's foray into the emerging electronically controlled SLR market. Most are silver, with black grip and chrome trim, but some are black with silver and trim. The AE-1 is a reliable and easy to use camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Canon AE-1 Program is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Canon in 1981. It is an upgraded version of the popular Canon AE-1, featuring a Program mode that automatically sets the aperture and shutter speed for easy shooting. The camera has a solid build with a metal body and a comfortable grip. It is powered by a single 4LR44 6V battery, which provides power to the metering system and the electronic shutter. The AE-1 Program has a bright and clear viewfinder with a split-image focusing aid and a microprism collar. It has a horizontal cloth focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 2 seconds to 1/1000th of a second, as well as a Bulb mode for long exposures. The camera supports interchangeable lenses and has a Canon FD lens mount. It also features a self-timer, exposure compensation, and a hot shoe for attaching an external flash. The AE-1 Program is a reliable and versatile camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Canon AV-1 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera introduced in 1979 by Canon Inc., using the FD lens mount system. Unlike the earlier Canon AE-1, the AV-1 features aperture-priority autoexposure, meaning the user sets the aperture and the camera automatically selects the appropriate shutter speed; the camera does not support fully manual exposure control. The AV-1 was developed in response to market demand, particularly from international distributors, for an aperture-priority SLR similar to models offered by competitors. The introduction of the AV-1 coincided with the release of Canon's New FD lenses, which allowed for quicker and easier lens changes through a simplified bayonet mounting system. The AV-1 is fully compatible with all accessories designed for the AE-1. AV in the model name stands for aperture value, reflecting the camera's emphasis on aperture-priority automation.

The Canon AF35M (also known as the Sure Shot in the USA) is a 35mm lens-shutter point-and-shoot camera introduced by Canon in November 1979 and notable as Canon’s first autofocus compact model. It employs an active triangulation autofocus system using a near-infrared emitter and photodiode, enabling accurate automatic focusing independent of ambient light. The camera’s fixed 38mm f/2.8 lens features manual ISO setting (25–400) around the lens barrel and utilizes a CdS photoresistor metering cell positioned inside the filter ring for reliable metering even with filters attached. Fully automatic film advance and rewind are provided, though film must be manually threaded onto the take-up spool. Other features include a built-in retractable flash with auto-exposure and fill-flash functions, projected framelines and indicators in the optical viewfinder, self-timer, and power supplied by two AA batteries. The AF35M measures 132 × 77 × 54 mm, weighs 405 g, and was manufactured in Japan, with production reaching up to 110,000 units per month by 1981.

The Canonet QL17 GIII is a compact rangefinder camera that was produced by Canon in the 1970s. It features a fixed 40mm f/1.7 lens, which is known for its sharpness and low-light capabilities. The camera has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings, and it offers both manual and automatic exposure modes. The QL17 GIII also has a quick-loading system, which allows for easy film loading and ensures smooth operation. With its compact size and reliable performance, the Canonet QL17 GIII is a popular choice among street photographers and enthusiasts.

The Canonet QL19 is a compact rangefinder camera produced by Canon in the 1960s. It features a fixed 45mm f/1.9 lens, which is known for its sharpness and low-light capabilities. The camera has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings, making it easy to capture well-exposed images. The QL in its name stands for Quick Loading, as it uses a unique film loading system that allows for fast and convenient film changes. The Canonet QL19 is a reliable and versatile camera that is perfect for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Canon Demi EE17 is a compact half-frame 35mm film camera manufactured by Canon and introduced in 1966. It uses standard 35mm film but exposes only half a frame per shot, allowing for 72 exposures on a 36-exposure roll. The camera features a fixed 30mm f/1.7 lens, which is notably fast for a half-frame camera. It is equipped with a CdS cell for automatic exposure control, offering shutter-priority auto-exposure as well as manual override. The shutter speeds range from 1/30 to 1/500 second, and the camera includes a built-in selenium light meter. Its compact size and fast lens made it popular for casual and travel photography.

The Canon EF is a 35mm single-lens reflex camera introduced by Canon in 1976. It is part of the Canon EOS system, which includes a wide range of interchangeable lenses and accessories. The EF features a rugged and durable construction, making it suitable for professional use. It has a built-in motor drive for advanced film transport, allowing for fast continuous shooting. The camera also has a large and bright viewfinder, providing a clear and accurate view of the subject. With its advanced autofocus system, the EF ensures sharp and precise focusing in various shooting conditions. It offers a wide range of exposure modes, including aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual mode, giving photographers full control over their images. The Canon EF is a versatile and reliable camera that delivers high-quality results.

The Canon EOS 1 is a professional 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Canon in 1989. It was the company's first professional-level EOS camera. The EOS-1 had a single centrally mounted autofocus point, plus basic weather sealing. The camera has a fixed eye-level pentaprism viewfinder has 100-percent vertical and horizontal coverage.

The Canon EOS 100 (Elan in America, EOS100 QD in Japan) is a 35mm autofocus SLR film camera that was released in August 1991. It is a mid-range 35mm autofocus SLR notable for introducing silent operation mechanisms in film advance and rewind, reducing noise to as little as one-eighth compared to earlier models. It uses the Canon EF lens mount system and features TTL phase-detection autofocus with both One-Shot AF and Predictive AI Servo AF, and a cross-type sensor for improved accuracy. The electronic shutter offers speeds from 30 seconds to 1/4000 second, alongside various auto and manual exposure modes including shutter-priority, aperture-priority, depth-of-field AE, and multiple program modes. The built-in flash automatically adjusts its coverage to match lens focal lengths (28mm, 50mm, and 80mm), and offers red-eye reduction, second-curtain sync, and flash exposure compensation. The camera provides advanced metering options with a 6-zone evaluative system and partial and center-weighted averaging, as well as a Quick Control Dial for real-time exposure adjustments while viewing through the viewfinder. Additional features include a 0.75x magnification pentaprism viewfinder, external LCD display for key settings, automatic film loading and rewind, support for multiple exposures and custom functions, all powered by a 6V lithium battery.

The Canon EOS 1N is a professional 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Canon in 1994. It is the successor to the EOS 1 and offers improved autofocus performance and advanced features. The EOS-1N was a revision of the EOS-1, with five autofocus points spread across the frame rather than a single centrally mounted autofocus point, plus more effective weather sealing, a wider exposure range, and numerous other improvements. The camera featured polycarbonate external construction with weather-resistant seals around buttons, dials, and its Canon EF lens mount.

The Canon EOS 1V is a professional 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Canon in 2000. It is the successor to the EOS 1N and offers improved autofocus performance and advanced features. The camera features a durable and weather-sealed magnesium alloy body, making it suitable for use in various shooting conditions. It has a 45-point autofocus system with 41 cross-type sensors, allowing for fast and accurate focusing. The EOS 1V also has a maximum shutter speed of 1/8000s and a continuous shooting speed of up to 10 frames per second, making it ideal for capturing fast-moving subjects. It has a built-in motor drive for advancing film and offers multiple exposure modes, including aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual mode. The camera is compatible with Canon EF lenses, providing a wide range of options for different shooting situations. Overall, the Canon EOS 1V is a reliable and versatile camera that is favored by professional photographers for its exceptional performance and durability.

The Canon EOS 3 is a professional-level 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Canon in 1998. It is part of the popular EOS series and is known for its advanced features and excellent performance. The camera features a durable and ergonomic design, with a comfortable grip and intuitive controls. It has a built-in motor drive and can shoot at a fast continuous shooting speed of up to 4.5 frames per second. The EOS 3 also boasts a highly accurate 45-point autofocus system, which ensures sharp and precise focus in various shooting conditions. It has a wide ISO range of 6 to 6400, allowing for versatile shooting in different lighting situations. The camera also offers multiple exposure modes, including aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual mode, giving photographers full control over their creative vision. With its robust construction and advanced features, the Canon EOS 3 is a reliable and versatile camera for professional photographers.

The Canon EOS 30, also known as the EOS Elan 7e in North America, is a 35mm autofocus SLR film camera introduced by Canon in 2000. It features an EF lens mount compatible with Canon's extensive range of EF lenses. The camera is equipped with a 7-point autofocus system and offers Eye-Controlled Focus, allowing users to select autofocus points by looking at them in the viewfinder. It supports shutter speeds from 30 seconds to 1/4000 second and has a built-in pop-up flash with E-TTL flash metering. The EOS 30 provides multiple exposure modes, including full manual, aperture priority, shutter priority, and program mode. Notable features include a quiet film advance mechanism and compatibility with Canon's battery grip BG-ED3.

The Canon EOS 33, also known as the EOS Elan 7 in North America, is a 35mm autofocus SLR film camera introduced by Canon in 2000. It features the Canon EF lens mount, supporting a wide range of Canon EF lenses. The camera offers a 7-point autofocus system and supports E-TTL flash metering for improved flash photography. Shutter speeds range from 30 seconds to 1/4000 second, with a maximum flash sync speed of 1/125 second. Notable features include silent drive operation, custom functions, and compatibility with battery grips. The EOS 33 is aimed at advanced amateurs seeking a reliable and versatile film SLR.

The Canon EOS 300 is a consumer-level 35mm single-lens reflex camera introduced by Canon in 1999. The autofocus capabilities of this camera were identical to Canon's much more expensive Elan 7 with six single-line CMOS sensors surrounding a central cross-type sensor. Upon its release, the Canon EOS 300 had the fastest autofocus and most advanced autoexposure in its class.

The Canon EOS 5, also known as the Canon EOS A2, is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera that was introduced by Canon in 1992. It is part of Canon's EOS series and features a sleek and ergonomic design. The EOS 5 offers advanced autofocus capabilities with its 45-point autofocus system, making it ideal for capturing fast-moving subjects. It also has a built-in motor drive, allowing for continuous shooting at up to 5 frames per second. The camera has a bright and clear viewfinder, making it easy to compose your shots. It also has a variety of exposure modes, including aperture priority, shutter priority, and program mode, giving you flexibility in your shooting. The Canon EOS 5 is a reliable and versatile camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Canon EOS 50 (Elan II in America, EOS 55 in Japan) is an autofocus, autoexposure 35mm SLR camera introduced in September 1995, targeting the advanced amateur market. The camera features a plastic body construction with aluminum-covered lens mount and top deck, along with a rear command dial and support for custom functions. Three variants were produced: the basic EOS 50, the EOS 50E with enhanced 3-zone eye-controlled autofocus, and the Japan-exclusive EOS 55 which offered an all-black color option and panorama mode that masks the frame to a 13mm x 36mm strip. The EOS 50 was the first camera to implement Canon's E-TTL flash system, which uses a pre-flash for metering rather than measuring light reflected from the film during exposure. An optional BP-50 battery grip with dedicated portrait shutter release was available, and all variants could be equipped with a quartz date imprint back. Production ended in October 2000 with the introduction of the EOS 30.

The Canon EOS 650 is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera that was introduced by Canon in 1987. It was the first EOS camera to feature both autoexposure and autofocus capabilities. The camera features a built-in motor drive, allowing for continuous shooting at up to 2 frames per second. It has a 5-point autofocus system and a TTL metering system that uses a 6-zone evaluative metering sensor. The EOS 650 also has a bright and clear viewfinder with a 0.82x magnification. It is compatible with Canon EF lenses and has a wide range of exposure modes, including program, aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual. The camera is powered by a 6V lithium battery and has a built-in flash with a guide number of 12. The Canon EOS 650 is a reliable and user-friendly camera that is suitable for both beginners and advanced photographers.

The Canon FX is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera introduced by Canon Inc. in April 1964. It was the first Canon camera to use the FL lens mount, following the earlier R mount system. The FX features a built-in CdS lightmeter located on the camera body (not through-the-lens) with selectable sensitivity ranges for different lighting conditions and supports film speeds from ISO 10 to 800. Its focal plane shutter offers speeds from 1 second to 1/1000 second in full-stop increments, and X-sync flash functionality is provided via a PC socket at 1/55 second. The viewfinder uses a glass pentaprism, providing approximately 90% vertical and 93% horizontal frame coverage at 0.9× magnification with a standard 50mm lens. Available historically in both silver and extremely rare all-black finishes, the FX remains a notable milestone in Canon’s transition toward modern SLR systems.

The Canon F-1 is a professional-level 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Canon in 1971. It was designed to compete with other high-end cameras of its time, such as the Nikon F series. The F-1 features a rugged and durable construction, with a metal body and a large, comfortable grip. It has a fully mechanical shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/2000 seconds, as well as a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control. The camera offers interchangeable viewfinders and focusing screens, allowing photographers to customize their shooting experience. With its wide range of compatible lenses and accessories, the Canon F-1 is a versatile camera that is well-suited for professional photographers and enthusiasts alike.

The Canon FTb is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera introduced by Canon in 1971. It is a manual focus camera that offers full manual control over exposure and focus. The FTb features a rugged and durable metal body, making it suitable for use in various shooting conditions. It has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings through the viewfinder. The camera uses Canon FD mount lenses, which are known for their excellent optical quality. The FTb also has a vertical-travel, metal-bladed focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/1000 to 1 second, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. With its reliable performance and classic design, the Canon FTb is a popular choice among film photography enthusiasts.

The Canon New F-1 is a professional-grade 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Canon in 1981. It is the successor to the original Canon F-1, and it was designed to meet the demands of professional photographers. The New F-1 features a rugged and durable construction, with a metal body and a large, comfortable grip. It has a bright viewfinder with a high-eyepoint design, which allows for easy and accurate framing of the subject. The camera offers a wide range of advanced features, including a through-the-lens (TTL) metering system, multiple exposure capability, and interchangeable focusing screens. It is compatible with a wide range of Canon FD lenses, giving photographers a versatile system to work with. The Canon New F-1 is highly regarded for its reliability, durability, and exceptional image quality.

The Canon P is a 35mm rangefinder camera introduced by Canon in 1959. It was designed as a more affordable alternative to the Canon VI-L. The camera features a durable and compact metal body with a black and chrome finish. It has a built-in coupled rangefinder that allows for precise focusing and a bright viewfinder for easy composition. The Canon P uses interchangeable screw-mount lenses and has a focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/1000 to 1 second, as well as bulb mode. It also has a self-timer and a flash sync socket for external flash units. The Canon P is known for its reliable performance and excellent image quality, making it a popular choice among photographers.

The Canon Autoboy S (also known as Prima Super 115, Sure Shot Z115) is a fully automatic 35mm zoom camera originally introduced in September 1993 as a top-of-the-line consumer point-and-shoot model. The camera features a 38-115mm f/3.6-8.5 zoom lens with 3x magnification, constructed with two molded glass aspherical elements for enhanced optical quality. It incorporates advanced features for its time including a high-speed 1/1200 second shutter with real-time release, AIAF with three-point measurement, and a rear mode dial for scene selection. The camera was marketed under different names across regions (Sure Shot Z115 in the Americas, Prima Super 115N globally, and Autoboy S in Japan) and received a white gold revision in March 1999. A newer variant, the Canon Sure Shot Z115 Panorama/Prima Super 115N/Autoboy S XL, was introduced in 1999 with additional features. The camera represents Canon's consumer-focused automatic photography technology of the mid-1990s, combining ease of use with relatively sophisticated optical and electronic systems.

The Canon T90 is a professional 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Canon in 1986. It was the last high-end manual focus camera produced by Canon before the transition to autofocus. The T90 features a rugged and durable body made of metal and plastic, with a comfortable grip for extended use. It has a bright and clear viewfinder with a 0.75x magnification, allowing for precise framing and focusing. The camera offers a wide range of exposure modes, including aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual mode, giving photographers full control over their images. It also has a built-in motor drive, capable of shooting up to 4.5 frames per second, making it suitable for action photography. The T90 is compatible with Canon FD lenses, providing a wide selection of high-quality optics. Overall, the Canon T90 is a reliable and versatile camera for professional photographers.

The Canonet QL 17 GIII is the final, high-end version of Canon's Canonet compact rangefinder series. It features shutter-priority auto-exposure and parallax compensation with its 40mm f/1.7 lens. The camera is small and dense, with rounded corners and a black leatherette. It was available in brushed nickel or solid black. Film advance, exposure counter, shutter release, rewind crank, and the hot shoe are located on the top plate. It uses one 1.35V M20 mercury battery or a modern equivalent and has a hot shoe with a proprietary contact for Canolite D, as well as a PC socket. The camera weighs 620g.

The Canon T70 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was released by Canon in April 1984. It was the second camera in Canon's T-series and was often sold with either an FD 35-70mm f/3.5-4.5 lens or an FD 28-55mm f/3.5-4.5 lens. The T70 features a vertical-traveling, electronic focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 2 seconds to 1/1000th of a second. It includes a built-in auto winder and a large LCD panel with key-touch buttons, which influenced subsequent 35mm SLR camera designs. The camera offers shutter-priority TTL auto exposure, TTL multi-program AE, and preset aperture AE, along with a dual metering system providing center-weighted averaging and partial metering. It is powered by two AA batteries and supports film speeds from 12 to 1600 ISO. The T70 received the Good Design Award and the European Camera of the Year Award in 1984.

The Canon EOS 500 is an entry-level 35mm autofocus SLR camera introduced by Canon in 1993. It was also known as the EOS Rebel XS in North America and the EOS Kiss in Japan. A similar model without a built-in flash was available as the EOS Rebel X. It features an electronic vertical travel focal plane shutter with speeds from 30 seconds to 1/2000th of a second and a built-in pop-up flash with a guide number of 12. The metering system uses a silicon photo diode with evaluative, central partial, and center-weighted average modes, and supports film speeds from 6 to 6400 ISO. Exposure modes include aperture priority, shutter priority, depth of field AE, manual exposure, and a program mode with scene selections. Film loading is automatic, prewinding the film onto the take-up spool, and it advances up to 3 frames per second. It is powered by two 3V CR123A lithium batteries.

The Canon TX is a 35mm SLR film camera that was released by Canon in 1975. It was a stripped-down version of the FTb, intended for export overseas and never sold in Japan. It features a center-weighted averaging light meter that is constantly active, a horizontal-travel cloth focal-plane shutter with a top speed of 1/500th, and a hot shoe with a single auto-switching FP and X flash sync PC terminal. Unlike the FTb, it lacks a metering switch, battery check, lockable stop-down lever, Quick Load system, mirror lock-up, and lockable shutter release. It was preceded by the similar TLb, which omitted the hot shoe.

The Canon AT-1 is a 35mm SLR film camera introduced by Canon in late 1976 as an export-only model. It shares the FD lens mount and many accessories with the AE-1 but is a match-needle, manual-exposure camera. Its viewfinder displays an analog needle for scene brightness, which the user aligns with an EV "lollipop" by adjusting aperture or shutter speed. The AT-1 uses an electronically timed shutter and is battery-dependent. It features a 10-second self-timer with an LED indicator. The AT-1 offers access to inexpensive, used FD-mount lenses in a body without extraneous features.

The Canon EOS 620 is a 35mm auto focus SLR camera introduced by Canon in 1987, shortly after the EOS 650. It shares many features with the EOS 650 but includes several improvements. The EOS 620 offers a faster maximum shutter speed of 1/4,000s, compared to the 1/2000s of the EOS 650. Its flash synchronization speed is also faster at 1/250s, an improvement over the 1/125s of the EOS 650. Additionally, the EOS 620 features an illuminated LCD screen. However, it does not include the automatic depth-of-field mode found on the EOS 650.

The Canon EOS 630, known as the EOS 600 in some markets, is an autofocus SLR camera introduced by Canon in 1989. It features motorized film advance and rewind, capable of reaching 5 frames per second in one-shot AF mode. The camera's shutter speeds range from 30 seconds to 1/2000 second, including a Bulb mode, and it has an X-sync speed of 1/125 second. It is powered by a single 6V 2CR5 lithium battery. The EOS 630 was also available with a quartz date back in some regions.

The Canon EX Auto is a 35mm SLR camera produced by Canon in 1972. It features a unique design where the rear lens group is fixed to the camera body, and various front lens groups can be attached via a screw fitting. This model is an improvement over the earlier EXEE, offering through-the-lens metering and shutter-priority automatic exposure. Unlike its predecessor, the EX Auto automatically detects the maximum aperture of the attached front lens groups. Shutter speed is set on a dial near the release button, while aperture is controlled by a dial around the rewind crank, with settings from f/1.8 to f/16, as well as 'Auto' and 'Off' positions. The camera has a horizontal cloth focal plane shutter with speeds from 1/8 to 1/500 second plus 'B', and X-synchronization for flash at 1/60 second. It also includes Canon's QL (Quick Load) feature for simplified film loading.

The Canon EOS 300X is an autofocus 35mm SLR camera manufactured by Canon and released in September 2004. It is known as the Rebel T2 in the US and the EOS Kiss 7 in Japan. This camera is the successor to the EOS 300V, Rebel Ti, and EOS Kiss 5. It features an EF lens mount, a focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 30 seconds to 1/4000th of a second, and an optical TTL viewfinder. The EOS 300X supports DX coded film from 25-5000 ISO and manual settings from 6-6400 ISO. It has an E-TTL II flash hotshoe, 35-zone exposure metering, and offers manual, aperture priority, and shutter priority exposure modes. Focusing is handled by a 7-point autofocus system with One Shot, AI, and AI Servo modes. It can shoot continuously at 3 frames per second and has a motorized film advance. The camera is powered by two CR2 lithium batteries.

The Canon T50 is a 35mm SLR camera introduced by Canon in March 1983. It was the first model in Canon's "T-series" of cameras. The T50 features powered film winding and programmed automatic exposure, and it is compatible with Canon FD mount lenses. Its vertical traveling electronic shutter operates at speeds from 2 seconds to 1/1000 second in automatic mode. The camera uses a TTL SPD photocell for metering, with an exposure value range of 1 to 18 EV at ISO 100. It supports film speeds from 50 to 1600 ISO. The T50 is powered by two AA/LR6 batteries, which provide enough power for approximately 50 rolls of 36-exposure film.

The Canon EOS 3000N is a 35mm film consumer SLR camera that was released by Canon in 2002. It was one of Canon's last 35mm film SLR bodies designed for Canon EF autofocus system lenses. This model is also known as the EOS Rebel XS N, EOS Rebel GII, and EOS 66 in other markets. It replaced the Canon EOS 3000 in the product line. The camera is noted for being lightweight and operating quietly. It features a range of operation modes, including fully automatic, semi-automatic, scene modes, and TTL flash modes. The EOS 3000N was later succeeded by the EOS 3000V.

The Canon EOS 1000F is a 35mm film SLR camera that was manufactured in Taiwan between 1991 and 1993. It is known as the EOS Rebel S in the Americas and the EOS 1000F in Europe and other regions, and features a built-in flash. This prosumer camera offers both auto-focus and auto-exposure capabilities. It includes a range of automatic, manual, and scene modes, such as sports, people, animals, landscapes, and macro. The EOS 1000F utilizes lenses with the EOS EF mount and was commonly sold with a 35-80mm f4-5.6 zoom lens. Its vertical-travel, focal-plane electronic shutter operates from 30 seconds to 1/1000 second plus Bulb, with X-sync up to 1/90 second via a hot shoe for Canon's TTL auto-exposure flash. Power is supplied by a 2CR5 6V battery.

The Canon Canonet 28 is a 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Canon in 1971. It features a fixed 40mm f/2.8 Canon lens and has fully programmed auto exposure with shutter speeds from 1/30 to 1/600. It also offers manual control of f-stops for flash. The camera uses a Copal leaf shutter and has a coupled rangefinder. It was manufactured in Taiwan and marketed until 1976. The Canonet 28 had a brief moment of Hollywood stardom, used by the title character of the 1998 John Waters film Pecker.

The Canon EOS 3000 is an autofocus SLR camera for 35mm film that was introduced by Canon in 1999. It was also sold as the EOS 88 in Asia. This model was not sold in the US. To keep it a lower-cost model, it features a pentamirror viewfinder and a manually-activated popup flash. It includes a full range of autoexposure modes, as well as off-the-film flash exposure setting. The camera has motorized film transport and requires two 3-volt CR123 lithium batteries to operate.

The Canon WP-1, also known as the Sure Shot A-1 or Prima AS-1, is a compact camera that was released in April 1994. It was marketed as the world's smallest and lightest underwater camera that could also be used on land. This fully automatic camera features a 32mm f/3.5 lens and a programmed shutter with speeds ranging from 1/250s to 1/60s. It incorporates 3-point smart autofocus for distances from 1-3m and a fixed focus macro mode for underwater shots as close as 45cm, which uses a forced flash. The camera is completely weather-sealed and robust, designed to be waterproof to five meters using rubber seals and O-rings. It has a large and bright viewfinder suitable for use with swimming goggles, an automatic flash that can be disabled, and automatic film winding. The WP-1 is powered by one 3V CR123A battery.

The Canon EOS 300V, also known as the Canon Rebel Ti, is a 35mm SLR film camera released in 2002 as an upgrade to Canon's EOS Rebel series. It is known for having the fastest autofocus and most advanced autoexposure in its class at the time of its release. The camera features a stainless steel lens mount, replacing the less durable plastic mounts of previous EOS Rebel cameras. It uses a TTL CMOS sensor with 7 AF points for autofocus and a TTL 35 zone SpD sensor for exposure, with a metering range of 1 to 20 EV. The electronic shutter offers speeds from 30 seconds to 1/2000 in 1/2 stop, plus bulb mode, and an X sync of 1/90s. It has a built-in flash with a guide number of 12 (ISO 100) and is powered by two 3V CR2 batteries.

The Canon EOS 500N is a 35mm SLR camera produced by Canon from 1996 to 1999. It is also known as the EOS Rebel G in the Americas and the New EOS Kiss or EOS Kiss 2 in Japan. This model replaced the EOS 500 and features a focal plane shutter with a range of 30 seconds to 1/2000th of a second, plus Bulb mode. It uses a Canon EF mount for lenses and has an optical pentaprism viewfinder. The camera is powered by two CR123A batteries and supports an ISO range of 6-6400 (25-5000 DX). Improvements over its predecessor include ETTL flash compatibility, an AF assist light, and Auto Exposure Bracketing (AEB) from -2 to +2 in 1/2 stop increments. It also features an easier-to-access night scene mode on the command dial and is compatible with the BP-8 vertical grip.

The Chamonix 45N-1 Classic is a lightweight 4x5 large format field camera designed for portability and versatility. Constructed from a combination of teak wood, carbon fiber, and anodized aluminum, it weighs approximately 1,470 grams and folds down to a compact size for travel. It offers full front movements (including rise, fall, shift, and axis tilt) and rear movements such as tilt and swing. The camera uses a rear-centered screw-drive focusing system, which provides smooth and precise focusing. With a maximum bellows draw of 395mm and support for a wide range of focal lengths, it's suitable for both beginners and experienced large format photographers. Priced competitively, the 45N-1 Classic is often favored by students and outdoor photographers seeking a balance of function and weight.

The Chamonix 810 Alpinist X is an ultralight, full-featured 8x10 field view camera designed for landscape and travel photographers. Built from anodized aluminum and wood, it offers rigidity, precision, and portability, weighing approximately 2,890 grams without the ground glass cover. The camera features extensive front and rear movements, including 87mm front rise, 75mm front fall, 50mm front shift (each side), 30° front tilt, and 30° rear tilt with 10° rear swing. Bellows extension ranges from a minimum of 60mm to a maximum of 850mm with an extension board, supporting a wide range of focal lengths. It folds down to a compact 355mm x 310mm x 97mm size and uses standard Sinar-type lens boards. As of late 2024, Chamonix also offers a compatible Fresnel lens and carbon fiber ground glass protector for improved focusing visibility in the field.

The Chinon 3001 is a compact 35mm film camera that was introduced in the 1980s. It features a fixed 38mm f/2.8 lens, which provides a versatile focal length for various shooting situations. The camera has a fully automatic exposure system, making it easy to use for beginners. It also has a built-in flash for low-light situations. The Chinon 3001 has a sleek and ergonomic design, with a comfortable grip for steady shooting. It is powered by two AA batteries, which are readily available. Overall, the Chinon 3001 is a reliable and user-friendly camera that is perfect for capturing everyday moments.

The Chinon CM-4 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera that was introduced in 1980. It features a solid and durable construction with a black metal body. The camera has a manual focus system and a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control. It offers a wide range of shutter speeds from 1 second to 1/1000th of a second, as well as a Bulb mode for long exposures. The CM-4 has a standard hot shoe for attaching an external flash and a self-timer for delayed shutter release. It is compatible with a variety of interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to explore different focal lengths and creative possibilities. Overall, the Chinon CM-4 is a reliable and versatile camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Contax 139 Quartz is a 35mm SLR film camera manufactured by Yashica/Kyocera under the Contax brand, first released in 1979. It features a quartz-timed electronically controlled vertical-travel metal focal plane shutter with speeds from 11 seconds to 1/1000 second plus Bulb. The camera uses the Contax/Yashica bayonet lens mount, supporting a wide range of Carl Zeiss T* lenses. It offers aperture-priority automatic exposure as well as full manual control, with through-the-lens (TTL) center-weighted metering. Notable features include a compact and lightweight body, electronic self-timer, and a viewfinder with LED exposure information. The Contax 139 Quartz is powered by two SR44 or LR44 batteries and includes a hot shoe for flash use.

The Contax 645 is a medium format film camera that was introduced by Contax in 1999. It is a popular choice among professional photographers for its exceptional image quality and versatile features. The camera features a modular design, allowing photographers to interchange different components such as the film back, viewfinder, and lenses. It has a 6x4.5cm film format, which offers a larger negative size compared to 35mm film cameras, resulting in sharper and more detailed images. The Contax 645 also boasts a reliable autofocus system, making it suitable for both studio and on-location shoots. With its ergonomic design and intuitive controls, it is a pleasure to use for extended periods of time. Overall, the Contax 645 is a reliable and high-performing camera that is favored by professionals in the fashion, portrait, and wedding photography industries.

The Contax G1 is a 35mm autofocus rangefinder camera that was introduced by Contax in 1994. It is part of the Contax G system, which was designed to compete with Leica's M series. The G1 features a unique electronic autofocus system that uses infrared sensors to measure the distance between the camera and the subject. It has a built-in motor drive for advancing the film and a motorized rewind function. The camera has a titanium body, which makes it lightweight and durable. The G1 has a wide range of compatible lenses, including a 28mm, 35mm, 45mm, 90mm, and a zoom lens. It also has a built-in flash and a hot shoe for external flash units. The G1 offers a variety of exposure modes, including aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual. It has a bright and clear viewfinder, and the rangefinder focusing system allows for precise focusing. The G1 is a highly regarded camera among film enthusiasts and is known for its exceptional image quality and reliable performance.

The Contax G2 is a high-end autofocus 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Kyocera in 1996. It is the successor to the Contax G1 and is known for its exceptional build quality and advanced features. The camera features a titanium body, making it lightweight and durable. It has a built-in motor drive and offers both aperture-priority and manual exposure modes. The G2 uses interchangeable lenses with a unique autofocus system that uses a secondary mirror to focus accurately. It has a maximum shutter speed of 1/6000s and a flash sync speed of 1/200s. The camera also has a built-in exposure meter and offers multiple exposure and exposure compensation capabilities. The Contax G2 is highly regarded for its superb image quality and precise autofocus performance.

The Contax IIIa is a 35mm rangefinder camera that was produced by the German manufacturer Zeiss Ikon from 1951 to 1962. It is a highly regarded camera known for its exceptional build quality and advanced features. The IIIa features a coupled rangefinder and viewfinder, allowing for precise focusing and composition. It is equipped with a Carl Zeiss Sonnar 50mm f/1.5 lens, which produces sharp and contrasty images. The camera has a top shutter speed of 1/1250 second, making it suitable for capturing fast-moving subjects. The IIIa also has a built-in light meter, which was a rare feature at the time. It uses a match needle system for exposure control, providing accurate and reliable metering. The Contax IIIa is a favorite among vintage camera enthusiasts and photographers who appreciate the timeless design and excellent performance of this classic rangefinder.

The Contax RTS is a professional-level 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Contax in 1975. It is part of the renowned Contax RTS series and was produced by Yashica under licence from Zeiss. The first RTS (short for Real Time System) was designed by Prof. Dr. Katsuiko Sugaya, styled by the Porsche Design studio, and manufactured by Yashica as Top Secret Project 130.

The Contax RTS II is a professional-level 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Contax in 1982. It is part of the renowned Contax RTS series and is highly regarded for its robust build quality and advanced features. The camera features a metal chassis and a durable titanium top cover, making it sturdy and reliable for professional use. It has a bright viewfinder with a split-image focusing screen and a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control. The RTS II offers full manual control as well as aperture-priority and program modes. It has a vertical metal shutter with a maximum speed of 1/2000th of a second and a flash sync speed of 1/125th of a second. The camera is compatible with a wide range of high-quality Carl Zeiss lenses, which are known for their exceptional optical performance. Overall, the Contax RTS II is a versatile and dependable camera that is highly sought after by both professional photographers and enthusiasts.

The Contax S2 is a manual focus 35mm film camera that was introduced by Contax in 1992. It is part of the Contax S series, which is known for its robust build quality and exceptional image quality. The S2 features a durable all-metal body with a sleek and ergonomic design, making it comfortable to hold and use for extended periods. It has a built-in light meter that offers accurate exposure readings, and its shutter speed range is from 1 second to 1/4000th of a second. The S2 also has a bright and clear viewfinder with a 0.74x magnification, allowing for precise composition. It uses Contax/Yashica mount lenses, which are renowned for their optical performance. Overall, the Contax S2 is a reliable and high-quality camera that is well-suited for professional photographers and enthusiasts who appreciate the craftsmanship of traditional film photography.

The Contax T2 is a high-end compact film camera that was first released in 1990. It is known for its exceptional build quality and advanced features, making it a popular choice among professional photographers and enthusiasts. The camera features a Carl Zeiss Sonnar 38mm f/2.8 lens, which delivers sharp and vibrant images. It also has a built-in flash and a range of automatic shooting modes, including aperture priority and program mode. The T2 has a sleek and compact design, with a titanium body and a sliding lens cover for protection. It offers precise autofocus and a fast 1/500s maximum shutter speed, allowing for capturing fast-moving subjects. The camera is powered by a lithium-ion battery and supports DX-coded film with automatic ISO setting. With its combination of excellent image quality and portability, the Contax T2 remains a highly sought-after camera for film photography.

The Contax T3 is a high-end compact film camera that was introduced in 2001. It is known for its exceptional build quality and advanced features. The camera features a Carl Zeiss Sonnar 35mm f/2.8 lens, which produces sharp and detailed images. It has a built-in flash and a range of shooting modes, including aperture priority and manual. The T3 has a titanium body, making it lightweight and durable. It has a sleek design with a retractable lens and a built-in lens cover. The camera has a fast and accurate autofocus system, making it suitable for capturing fast-moving subjects. It also has a spot metering mode for precise exposure control. The T3 has a built-in motor drive for quick film advance and rewind. It uses 35mm film and has a standard ISO range of 25-5000. The camera has a bright and clear viewfinder for easy composition. Overall, the Contax T3 is a highly regarded camera among professionals and enthusiasts for its excellent image quality and compact size.

The Contax TVS is a premium 35mm compact zoom camera introduced by Kyocera under the Contax brand in 1994, during a period of intense competition in the luxury compact camera market. Notable for its titanium body, the TVS features a Carl Zeiss Vario-Sonnar 28-56mm f/3.5–6.5 zoom lens, providing high-quality optics and a versatile focal range suitable for everyday, travel, and street photography. The camera offers a blend of manual controls—including physical dials for exposure compensation and focus, and an aperture ring on the lens—alongside electronic LCD displays showing key settings in both the viewfinder and on the camera top plate. Autofocus operation is fast and accurate, with manual focus options available; exposure metering is center-weighted, with a spot meter in manual mode and an override dial allowing up to ±5 stops of compensation. The TVS is powered by a single CR123 battery and accepts 30.5mm filters (metering is not TTL, so exposure compensation may be needed when using filters). Distinctive for its tactile zoom control (via a physical lens barrel tab, which also serves as the on/off switch), the TVS balances electronic features with user-friendly ergonomics. The overall build is robust at just over 400 grams loaded, and it includes practical details such as a traditional lens cap, a panoramic mode, and a bright viewfinder with parallax compensation. Image quality is recognized for high contrast, low distortion, and accurate color rendition, with best sharpness found at mid-zoom and moderate apertures. Reliability concerns are noted, particularly regarding the internal ribbon cable connecting the lens—an electronic point of failure common to Contax compacts of this era, which may be challenging to repair due to age and complexity. The Contax TVS remains a notable example of high-end compact film camera design, valued for its combination of portability, precise controls, and optical performance.

The Contax Aria is a manual focus 35mm SLR camera produced by Kyocera/Yashica in 1998. It utilizes the Contax/Yashica MM lens mount. The camera features a vertical traveling focal-plane shutter with speeds ranging from 30 seconds to 1/4000 second, including a Bulb mode, with specific speed ranges depending on the shooting mode. It offers five exposure modes: Program, aperture-priority, shutter-priority, metered manual, and flash/TTL auto flash. Metering options include evaluative (Matrix), center-weighted, and spot metering. The Aria has a motorized film transport with automatic loading and mid-roll rewind capability, and two drive modes allowing for continuous shooting up to 3 frames per second. It supports DX coded film from 25 to 5000 ISO, and manual ISO settings from 6 to 6400. Power is supplied by two 3V CR2 batteries. A limited edition "70 Years" version was released in 2002.

The Contax RX is a 35mm single-lens reflex camera body with auto exposure modes and the Contax/Yashica MM lens mount. It was manufactured by Kyocera in 1994. The camera features an electromechanical shutter with speeds from 16 seconds to 1/4000 seconds. It supports aperture-priority, shutter speed-priority, programmed auto exposure, and manual exposure, along with TTL and manual flash control. Its TTL-metering is switchable between center-weighted and spot. The RX also includes a built-in TTL phase difference detection system for focusing, automatic film handling, a status LCD, AE-lock, and a 10-second self-timer. It offers continuous shooting at three images per second.

The Contax T is a high-quality, compact 35mm rangefinder camera introduced in 1984 and manufactured by Kyocera in Japan. It features a manually focused Carl Zeiss Sonnar 38mm f/2.8 lens that retracts into the camera body and is covered by a hinged lens cover. The camera utilizes an electronic between-the-lens shutter with speeds from 8 seconds to 1/500th, automatically set by its aperture priority exposure system. Designed by F.A. Porsche, the body incorporates titanium, and it features a synthetic ruby shutter release. It came with a dedicated Contax T14 electronic flash unit that attaches to the side. Film advance is manual, and it has an electronic frame counter with an LCD display. The Contax T has gained a cult status and was available in silver or black.

The Exakta HS-10 is a rebadging of the Cosina CT-1 EX. It is a manual focus 35mm SLR camera that accepts K-mount bayonet lenses and features a vertically-traveling metal focal-plane shutter with speeds from 1 second to 1/1000 second plus bulb mode. It incorporates an open-aperture TTL match-needle center-weighted metering system using a CdS cell, with a range of 3-18 EV at ASA 100 and film speed settings from 25-1600 ASA. The camera includes a mechanical self-timer with approximately 10-second delay and flash sync at 1/125 second. Originally designed for 1.35V mercury batteries (now banned), it will give incorrect meter readings with standard 1.5V alkaline or silver-oxide replacements.

The Exakta VX is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera that was produced by Ihagee in the 1950s. It is known for its robust build quality and advanced features for its time. The camera features a vertically traveling cloth focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/1000 to 1 second, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. It has a pentaprism viewfinder with a built-in light meter, which was a unique feature at the time. The Exakta VX also has interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to use a wide range of focal lengths. Overall, the Exakta VX is a reliable and versatile camera that is highly regarded by film photography enthusiasts.

The EB 617 MK II is a fully assembled 3D printed large format view camera offered by Film Laundry as a build-to-order option. The camera measures 28cm wide × 17cm deep × 22.5cm high and weighs 1.6kg, with an included film back that measures 27.5cm × 11.5cm × 4cm and weighs 500g. It accepts Linhof Technika style lens boards (96×99mm) and comes complete with film back and ground glass, requiring only the addition of a lens to be ready for use. The camera is based on plans that are also available separately for DIY builders who prefer to construct their own version. Film Laundry also offers a hardware kit option starting at $150 USD for those who want to 3D print the parts themselves but avoid sourcing individual components. This represents a modern approach to large format photography, combining traditional view camera functionality with contemporary 3D printing technology.

The Franka Solida II is a medium format folding camera produced by Franka-Kamerawerk in Germany, first introduced around 1950. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm images. The camera features a collapsible bellows design and is typically equipped with a Frankar-Anastigmat 75mm f/4.5 lens, though some variants may have different lenses or shutters. Shutter options commonly include Prontor or Vario shutters with speeds up to 1/200s. The Solida II is equipped with a simple optical viewfinder and manual film advance via a red window. Its compact, folding design made it popular for amateur photographers seeking portability and medium format quality.

The Fujica AZ-1 is a 35mm SLR camera produced by Fuji Photo Film Co. in the late 1970s. It features a fully electronic shutter with speeds ranging from 2 seconds to 1/1000th of a second, as well as a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control. The camera has a focal plane shutter and a pentaprism viewfinder, providing a bright and clear view of the scene. It has a bayonet lens mount, allowing for a wide range of interchangeable lenses to be used. The AZ-1 also has a self-timer function and a hot shoe for attaching an external flash. With its compact and lightweight design, the Fujica AZ-1 is a versatile and reliable camera for both beginner and advanced photographers.

The Fuji GA645 is a medium format film camera that offers a perfect balance between portability and image quality. It features a fixed 60mm f/4 lens, which provides a versatile focal length for a wide range of photography genres. The camera has an autofocus system that ensures sharp and accurate focus, and it also offers manual focus override for more control. The GA645 has a built-in light meter that helps in achieving proper exposure, and it supports both aperture priority and manual exposure modes. It has a bright and clear viewfinder for easy composition, and it also has a built-in flash for low-light situations. The camera is lightweight and compact, making it suitable for travel and on-the-go photography. Overall, the Fuji GA645 is a reliable and user-friendly medium format camera that delivers exceptional image quality.

The Fuji GA645i is a medium format film camera that was introduced by Fuji in 1997. It features a fixed 60mm f/4 lens, which provides a focal length equivalent to 35mm in 35mm format. The camera has an autofocus system that uses a passive infrared sensor for quick and accurate focusing. It also has a built-in light meter that measures the scene and sets the exposure automatically. The GA645i has a fully automatic mode, as well as aperture priority and manual exposure modes for more control over the exposure settings. It has a built-in motor drive that advances the film automatically, and it can also be used with a motorized film back for continuous shooting. The camera has a bright and clear viewfinder that shows the focusing distance, exposure information, and other settings. It has a built-in flash that can be used in various modes, including red-eye reduction. The GA645i is a versatile and easy-to-use camera that is well-suited for both professional and amateur photographers.

The Fuji GF670W is a medium format rangefinder camera capable of shooting both 6x7 (56x69mm) and 6x6 (56x56mm) images using 120 or 220 roll film, allowing up to 24 exposures on a single roll. It features a fixed, wide-angle EBC Fujinon 55mm f/4.5 lens with a manually controlled helicoid focus that covers from 0.7m to infinity and utilizes a coincidence-type rangefinder focusing mechanism with automatic parallax correction. The camera offers both aperture-priority auto-exposure and manual exposure modes, with metering sensitivity from EV1.3 to EV18 at ISO 100 and exposure compensation of +/-2 EV in 1/3 stop increments. Its electronically-controlled leaf shutter offers speeds from 4 seconds to 1/500 second, and syncs with flash at all speeds via hot shoe or X-synch terminal. Distinguishing itself from its sibling, the folding Fuji GF670, the GF670W has a fixed lens and lacks bellows, catering to photographers who prefer immediate readiness without unfolding the camera. The GF670W is closely related to the Voigtlander Bessa III/667W, with which it shares design and function, differing mainly in finish and branding.

The Fujica GS645W is a medium format rangefinder camera that was introduced by Fujifilm in 1984. It features a wide-angle 45mm f/5.6 lens, which is equivalent to a 28mm lens in 35mm format. The camera has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control and a bright viewfinder for easy composition. It has a fully manual operation, allowing photographers to have full control over their settings. The GS645W is known for its compact and lightweight design, making it a great choice for travel and street photography. It produces high-quality images with excellent sharpness and detail. Overall, the Fujica GS645W is a reliable and versatile medium format camera that is loved by many film photographers.

The Fuji GSW690 is a fully mechanical medium format rangefinder camera, designed for professional use and introduced as the first iteration of the GSW690 series in 1978. It features a fixed EBC Fujinon SW 65mm f/5.6 lens (providing a field of view equivalent to 28mm on 35mm film) and uses a Copal-type leaf shutter with speeds from T and 1s up to 1/500s. The camera shoots 6x9 cm images on 120 or 220 roll film, with selectable frame counters for 4, 8, or 16 exposures per roll, depending on film type. With no built-in light meter and entirely manual controls, the GSW690 emphasizes mechanical reliability and photographic basics. The viewfinder is clear with a vernier-style rangefinder patch for focusing, and the camera body, weighing approximately 1485 grams, is constructed from a die-cast metal frame clad with some plastic. Known for its large negative size and sharp fixed lens, the GSW690 is popular for landscape and panoramic work, and its straightforward operation makes it a favored tool for film photography enthusiasts seeking high image quality in a rangefinder format.

The Fuji GSW690II is a fully mechanical medium format rangefinder camera, designed for professional use and introduced as the second iteration of the GSW690 series. It features a fixed EBC Fujinon SW 65mm f/5.6 lens (providing a field of view equivalent to 28mm on 35mm film) and uses a Copal-type leaf shutter with speeds from T and 1s up to 1/500s. The camera shoots 6x9 cm images on 120 or 220 roll film, with selectable frame counters for 4, 8, or 16 exposures per roll, depending on film type. With no built-in light meter and entirely manual controls, the GSW690II emphasizes mechanical reliability and photographic basics. The viewfinder is clear with a vernier-style rangefinder patch for focusing, and the camera body, weighing approximately 1485 grams, is constructed from a die-cast metal frame clad with some plastic. Known for its large negative size and sharp fixed lens, the GSW690II is popular for landscape and panoramic work, and its straightforward operation makes it a favored tool for film photography enthusiasts seeking high image quality in a rangefinder format.

The Fujifilm GSW690III is a medium-format rangefinder film camera that produces 6x9 cm negatives, among the largest available in roll film photography. Introduced in the 1990s as part of the Fujifilm GW series, the GSW690III features a fixed Fujinon EBC 65mm f/5.6 wide-angle lens (approximately equivalent to a 28mm lens on 35mm format), optimized for landscape, studio, and travel photography. The lens is constructed with 6 elements in 4 groups, offers apertures from f/5.6 to f/32, and shutter speeds ranging from 1 second to 1/500 second, plus a T (time) mode for long exposures, all controlled via rings on the lens barrel. The camera operates fully manually: it lacks a built-in light meter or autofocus, and does not require batteries except for an optional flash. Film advance and frame counting are entirely mechanical, and the camera supports both 120 and (historically) 220 film formats, giving 8 exposures per 120 roll in 6x9 format. Notable features include a hot shoe, robust but somewhat plasticky body weighing approximately 1,510g, and dual shutter release buttons for ergonomic flexibility. The GSW690III employs a rangefinder focusing system and has some minor parallax error, as is typical for this type. It is well known for delivering exceptionally sharp, detailed images with high-resolution negatives, though its fixed wide lens limits versatility for some applications. Nicknamed the 'Texas Leica' for its large size and classic rangefinder style, the GSW690III has become increasingly scarce and expensive on the secondhand market.

The Fujica GW690 is a medium format film camera that was first introduced in 1978. It is a rangefinder camera that uses 120/220 roll film, allowing for larger negative sizes compared to 35mm cameras. The GW690 features a fixed lens with a focal length of 90mm, which provides a moderate wide-angle perspective. It has a bright and clear viewfinder with a built-in rangefinder for accurate focusing. The camera has a fully mechanical design, including manual film advance and shutter cocking. It offers a wide range of shutter speeds from 1/500 to 1 second, as well as bulb mode for long exposures. The GW690 is known for its robust build quality and reliable performance, making it a popular choice among professional photographers and enthusiasts who appreciate the exceptional image quality and control offered by medium format photography.

The Fuji GW690II is a medium format film camera known for its exceptional image quality and large negative size. It features a fixed 90mm f/3.5 lens, which is equivalent to a 35mm lens on a full-frame camera. The camera has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control, and a manual focus system for precise focusing. It has a simple and robust design, with a metal body and a large bright viewfinder. The GW690II uses 120 roll film, allowing for 8 exposures per roll. It is a popular choice among professional photographers and enthusiasts who appreciate the high-quality results and the unique look that medium format film provides.

The Fuji GW690III is a fixed-lens, medium format rangefinder camera introduced by Fuji in 1992 as the last model in their line of 6x9cm cameras. It is known for producing large 6x9cm negatives, offering some of the highest image resolution available in medium format cameras that use 120 film (yielding 8 exposures per roll). The camera features a manual, battery-free operation with a hotshoe for flash and a PC sync socket, but does not include a built-in meter. Its lens is an EBC Fujinon 90mm f/3.5 with five elements in five groups and a focal length equivalent to approximately a 40-45mm lens in 35mm terms. Weighing 1510g, the GW690III is often referred to as the 'Texas Leica' due to its large size relative to Leica rangefinders. Notable design details include aperture and shutter speed adjustment rings located on the lens, a T mode for long exposures (distinct from typical Bulb mode operation), and a loud mechanical exposure counter.

The Fujifilm GX680 is a professional medium format SLR camera system introduced in 1987. It uses 120/220 roll film to produce 6x8 cm images, and is notable for its modular design, allowing interchangeable lenses, film backs, and viewfinders. The GX680 features a unique bellows focusing system with front and rear standard movements, enabling tilt, shift, and swing adjustments for perspective and focus control. It offers electronic leaf shutter lenses with speeds up to 1/400 sec and supports both manual and aperture-priority auto exposure modes. The camera includes motorized film advance and an integrated rotating back for easy switching between portrait and landscape orientation. The GX680 system is highly regarded for studio and architectural photography due to its flexibility and image quality.

Fujifilm INSTAX Mini 90 Classic Instant Camera is a compact camera that produces credit card-sized prints. It features a retractable 60mm lens  that focuses up to 11.8 away, automatic exposure , and a  built-in flash for low-light conditions. The camera has an optical viewfinder with a target spot and digital controls, offering  6 shooting modes  and brightness control. It also has a  rechargeable battery  and displays the number of exposures remaining. This instant camera is ideal for capturing life's memories in a classic way, with its compact design and easy-to-use features making it perfect for scrapbooking or displaying on the refrigerator.

Fujifilm INSTAX mini 99 Instant Camera lets users unleash their artistic flair and create unique images for a true analog experience. Enhance your images using six available Color Effect settings, or use the 'normal' setting to render things as they are. There are also five shooting modes, including Normal, Indoor, Sports, Double Exposure, and Bulb, each of which helps to further optimize the camera for a particular shot and scene. If you feel a particular scene would benefit from additional highlight or shadow detail, you'll be able to choose from five levels of adjustable brightness. Or, leave the brightness set to 'normal' to keep things how they are. After you've taken a shot, images are printed on 2 x 3 INSTAX MINI instant film, which is sold separately.

The Fujifilm Klasse S is a premium compact 35mm film camera released primarily in Japan in mid-2007. It uses standard 135 (35mm) film with a frame size of 24mm x 36mm and is equipped with a 38mm f/2.8 Super EBC Fujinon lens. The camera features both autofocus (AF, 0.4m to infinity) and manual focus modes, with an optical viewfinder providing an 85% field of view. Exposure options include Program AE and Aperture Priority AE, supported by an electronic shutter with speeds ranging from bulb, 1/2s to 1/1000s, depending on the aperture setting. The Klasse S offers exposure compensation up to ±2.0 EV in 0.5 EV steps, DX-coded automatic and manual ISO selection from 25 to 3200, and an LCD display with backlight. Powered by a single 3v CR2 lithium battery, the camera measures 123 × 63.5 × 38.5mm and weighs 265g excluding the battery.

The Fujifilm Klasse W is a premium 35mm compact film camera that released in 2007 and is the wide angle version of the Fujifilm Klasse S. It is notable for its wide-angle 28mm f/2.8 Super EBC Fujinon lens. It supports both automatic (AF) and manual focus, with a minimum focusing distance of 0.3 meters. The camera offers multiple exposure modes, including Program AE and AE Aperture Priority, with apertures from f/2.8 to f/16 selectable via a physical dial. Its electronic shutter provides speeds from bulb and 1/2 s up to 1/1000 s, depending on the selected aperture. The Klasse W features auto DX-code film speed detection (ISO 25–3200) and allows manual ISO setting as well. Measuring 123 × 63.5 × 38.5 mm and weighing 270g (without battery), it is powered by a single CR2 lithium battery and includes a backlit LCD, self-timer, and ±2 EV exposure compensation via a front dial.

The Fujica ST801 is a 35mm manual single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera manufactured by Fuji from 1972 to 1978. It is notable for being the first 35mm SLR to feature a viewfinder LED display for light metering, replacing the traditional needle-based system with an electronic centre-indicator-light arrangement. The camera uses an M42 screw mount, with a Fuji modification enabling open-aperture metering via a small aperture coupling tab on compatible Fujinon lenses. Its through-the-lens (TTL) metering system employs silicon photocells for greater sensitivity and faster response than earlier CdS-based systems, and the metering results are displayed with a series of seven LEDs in the viewfinder. The camera supports shutter speeds up to 1/2000 second and offers open-aperture metering with matched Fujinon lenses, though stop-down metering is required for other M42 lenses. Additional features include a very bright viewfinder and compact body design for its era, but flash synchronization is limited to 1/60 second and the aperture coupling tab on some Fujinon lenses can cause compatibility issues with other M42 cameras and adapters.

The Fujifilm TX-1 is a 35mm film rangefinder camera introduced in 1998, developed in collaboration with Hasselblad (where it was also sold as the XPan). It features a unique dual-format capability, allowing photographers to switch between standard 24x36mm and panoramic 24x65mm frames on standard 35mm film. The camera uses interchangeable lenses with a dedicated lens mount and offers manual focus operation. It is equipped with an electronically controlled, vertical-travel focal plane shutter with speeds from 8s to 1/1000s plus Bulb mode. The TX-1 includes aperture-priority auto exposure and manual exposure modes, with through-the-lens (TTL) metering. Its robust titanium body and panoramic capabilities make it notable among film rangefinders.

The Fuji GS645S Professional Wide60 is a medium format rangefinder camera released on October 1, 1984. It features a newly-designed EBC Fujinon W 60mm f/4 Orthometar-type lens, which is comprised of 7 elements in 5 groups and is mounted in a mechanical Copal 00 shutter. This 60mm lens is equivalent to a 35mm lens in 35mm format and has a 49mm filter thread. The camera's lens is protected by a circular "cow bar." It has a built-in light meter with a measuring range of 4 to 18 EV, and ISO can be set from 25 to 1600 in 1/3 stops. The finder contains a coupled double image rangefinder for focusing, offering 0.5x magnification with a 40mm baseline, resulting in a 20mm effective baseline. The GS645S uses 120 and 220 film in a 6x4.5 format and is known for its sharp lenses.

The Fujica Panorama G617 is a medium format roll film panorama camera introduced by Fuji in 1983. A renamed model, the Fuji Panorama G617, was released in 1985. It captures photos in a 6x17cm format onto 120 or 220 film, yielding 4 or 8 exposures respectively. The camera features an EBC Fujinon SW 105mm f/8 lens with a 77mm filter thread. The manually cocked Seiko shutter, located within the lens, offers speeds from 1 second to 1/500th of a second, plus a bulb mode. It has a sync connector for flash, with electronic flash sync available at all shutter speeds. The camera includes a four-stroke film advance lever, two shutter releases, two accessory shoes, and a spirit level. Strap connectors allow for horizontal or vertical carrying.

The Fujifilm GF670, also known as the Voigtländer Bessa III, is a folding camera that takes 6x6cm or 6x7cm exposures on 120 or 220 film. It was jointly developed by Fujifilm and Cosina. This camera features a Fujinon or Heliar 80/3.5 lens, a coupled rangefinder, and offers aperture-priority automatic and manual exposure modes, along with an exposure compensator. Film is advanced via a knob, and it includes a hot shoe and a PC synch socket. The design of its front standard is similar to 1950s Voigtländer models.

The Fujica GL690 Professional is a medium-format, interchangeable-lens, leaf-shutter rangefinder camera released by Fuji Photo Film Co. in January 1974. It features a second shutter button on the front for vertical shooting and adds short-roll 120 film capability. The viewfinder magnification was increased from 84% to 92%, and the eyepiece was changed to a circular form, allowing the use of standard diopter lenses and other accessories. Cosmetic changes include the addition of "Professional" on top and a large stylized "G" on the lens mount. The focusing grips on the lenses are now rubber. A 50mm lens, a faster 65mm lens, and an autoexposure 100mm f/3.5 lens were released concurrently with the GL690.

The Fujica ST605N is a 35mm SLR camera made in Japan by Fuji, released in 1978. It is an updated version of the ST605, with the shutter speed setting indicated by a viewfinder pointer. It accepts Praktica/Pentax screwmount lenses and features a rubberized silk curtain focal plane shutter with speeds from 1/2 to 1/700s, plus B. It has stopped-down TTL center-weighted averaging metering via two Silicon photo-cell receptors coupled to a FET circuit, and a viewfinder center-the-needle exposure setting system. Focusing is via a central split image rangefinder, with a surrounding micro-prism area and ground glass. DOF preview is available via stop-down metering.
