The Fujica GS645 Professional is a folding rangefinder camera released in March 1983. It features an EBC Fujinon S 75mm f/3.4 lens with 5 elements and a closest focus distance of 1m. The camera uses a bellows for focusing and has a coupled double image rangefinder. Its light meter has a measuring range of 3.5 to 18 EV and can be set from 25 to 1600 ISO. The GS645 takes 120 and 220 film in a 6x4.5 format and is known for its sharp lenses. When folded, its depth is 56mm, and it weighs 820g without batteries.

The Fujifilm DL-100, also known as the Discovery S100 in America, is a basic autofocus camera released by Fuji in 2002. It features a Fujinon 32mm f/4.5 lens and a built-in flash. The camera operates on two AA alkaline batteries and includes motor wind and rewind for film transport. It is noted for its extra-large viewfinder, a common feature among its competitors. The autofocus system, paired with its wide and slow lens, can be inconsistent. This model should not be confused with the earlier Fujica DL-100. It was positioned as a budget-friendly option in the market.

The Fuji GW680III Professional is a medium-format rangefinder camera that uses 120/220 film. It is part of a series of cameras that succeeded Fuji's interchangeable-lens Fujica GL690 and GM670 Professional models. The GW680III, along with other models in the series, features a fixed lens, a design choice made to reduce weight and increase reliability, as sales of other focal lengths were low. The camera has a redesigned exterior with curves and rubberized coatings, and includes a small spirit level embedded in the top. It also features a push-button spool release. The GW680III differs from the GW690III only in having a smaller film gate and different gearing and numbering for the film advance mechanism.

The Graflex Pacemaker 45 Crown Graphic is a 4×5 large-format press camera produced from 1947 to 1973 and known for its iconic presence in mid-century photography and film. It features a leaf-shutter lens system, double-extension bellows for close-focus capability, and multiple focusing/composition options including ground glass, optical viewfinder with masks, and an optional rangefinder. Despite its portability and durable folding-bed design, camera operation is methodical and slow, often requiring tripod use and careful step-by-step handling. Front movements are limited to rise, tilt-up, and shift, making it less versatile than full view cameras for perspective control. Collectors and users value its flexibility with lenses, Graflok compatibility, and the high image quality achievable on 4×5 sheet film or roll-film backs.

The Graflex Speed Graphic is a large format camera that was first introduced in 1912. It is a versatile and durable camera that has been widely used by professional photographers for many decades. The Speed Graphic features a focal plane shutter, which allows for a wide range of shutter speeds, from 1/1000th of a second to several seconds. It has a bellows system that allows for adjustments in focus and perspective, making it ideal for architectural and landscape photography. The camera uses sheet film in various sizes, including 4x5 inches and 5x7 inches, and has a ground glass back for composing and focusing the image. The Speed Graphic also has a range of interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to choose the lens that best suits their needs. It is a heavy and bulky camera, but its robust construction and versatility make it a popular choice among large format photographers.

The Hasselblad 203FE is a medium format film camera that was introduced in 2002. It is part of Hasselblad's 200 series, which are known for their modular design and high-quality optics. The 203FE features a built-in electronic shutter, allowing for precise exposure control and faster shooting speeds. It has a focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/2000s to 32s, as well as a leaf shutter with speeds up to 1/800s. The camera uses interchangeable film magazines, allowing photographers to easily switch between different film types and formats. The 203FE is compatible with Hasselblad's wide range of lenses, which offer exceptional image quality and versatility. It also has a built-in motor drive for advanced film transport and continuous shooting. With its robust build quality and advanced features, the Hasselblad 203FE is a reliable and versatile choice for professional photographers.

The Hasselblad 500C is a legendary medium format film camera that was introduced in 1957. It is widely regarded as one of the most iconic cameras in the photography world. The 500C features a modular design with interchangeable lenses, viewfinders, and film backs, allowing photographers to customize the camera according to their needs. It uses 120 or 220 roll film and produces square 6x6cm negatives. The camera has a focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/500 to 1 second, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. It offers a waist-level viewfinder for composing images and a bright focusing screen for precise manual focusing. The Hasselblad 500C is known for its exceptional build quality, reliable mechanics, and superb image quality, making it a favorite among professional photographers and enthusiasts alike.

The Hasselblad 500C/M is a medium format film camera that was introduced in 1970 as an upgraded version of the original 500C. It is renowned for its modular design and exceptional image quality, making it a popular choice among professional photographers. The 500C/M features a focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/500 seconds, and interchangeable film backs that allow for easy film changing in the middle of a shoot. It also has a waist-level viewfinder, which provides a unique and immersive shooting experience. The camera uses 120 or 220 roll film, and with its interchangeable lenses, it offers a wide range of creative possibilities. The Hasselblad 500C/M is a reliable and versatile camera that has stood the test of time.

The Hasselblad 501CM is a medium format film camera that was introduced in 1997 as an updated version of the classic Hasselblad 500 series. It is a modular camera system known for its exceptional image quality and robust build. The 501CM features a 6x6cm square format and uses interchangeable film backs, lenses, and viewfinders. It has a manual focus system with a bright and clear waist-level viewfinder, allowing for precise composition. The camera has a leaf shutter mechanism, which provides a wide range of shutter speeds from 1 second to 1/500th of a second. It also offers a bulb mode for long exposures. The 501CM is compatible with a wide range of Hasselblad V System lenses, renowned for their sharpness and optical performance. It is a favorite among professional photographers and enthusiasts who value the timeless design and exceptional image quality of Hasselblad cameras.

The Hasselblad 503CX is a medium format single-lens reflex (SLR) camera introduced by Hasselblad in 1988. It uses 120 or 220 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The camera features a modular design, allowing interchangeable film backs, viewfinders, and lenses using the Hasselblad V-system bayonet mount. Notable technical improvements over its predecessor include an improved acute-matte focusing screen and built-in TTL (through-the-lens) flash metering. The 503CX is fully mechanical but requires a battery for the TTL flash metering system. It is renowned for its robust build quality and is widely used in professional studio and field photography.

The Hasselblad H2 is a professional medium format camera system introduced by Hasselblad in 2005. It supports both 120/220 roll film and digital backs, making it a hybrid platform for film and digital photography. The H2 features an autofocus system, electronically controlled focal plane shutter with speeds from 18 hours to 1/800s, and compatibility with Hasselblad HC and HCD lenses. It offers advanced metering options, including spot, center-weighted, and average metering. The camera includes integrated flash control and a modular design for interchangeable viewfinders, film backs, and grips. Notable for its ergonomic handling and system flexibility, the H2 was designed for professional studio and field use.

The Hasselblad SWC is a medium format film camera known for its wide-angle capabilities and exceptional image quality. It was first introduced in 1954 and quickly gained popularity among professional photographers for its compact size and high-performance optics. The SWC features a fixed 38mm Biogon lens, which provides a 90-degree field of view, making it ideal for landscape, architectural, and interior photography. The camera has a robust mechanical design and is built to withstand harsh shooting conditions. It offers a range of shutter speeds, from 1 second to 1/500th of a second, and has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control. The SWC uses 120 roll film, allowing for 6x6 square format images. With its exceptional image quality and wide-angle capabilities, the Hasselblad SWC remains a favorite among photographers who appreciate the unique perspective it offers.

The Hasselblad Xpan is a unique panoramic film camera that was introduced in 1998. It features a dual-format system, allowing photographers to switch between standard 35mm format and panoramic format by simply rotating the film back. The camera is equipped with a high-quality 45mm f/4 lens, providing sharp and detailed images. It also has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control. The Xpan offers a range of manual controls, including aperture and shutter speed settings, allowing photographers to have full creative control over their shots. With its sleek and compact design, the Xpan is a versatile camera that is perfect for capturing breathtaking panoramic landscapes and wide-angle scenes.

The Hasselblad 503CW is a 6x6 SLR medium format film camera introduced in 1996. It was the final model in a series that began with the 1957 Hasselblad 500 C. This fully mechanical camera is compatible with C, CF, CB, CFI, and CFE lenses, which feature leaf shutters. These lens shutters offer speeds ranging from 1 second to 1/500th, as well as a bulb mode. While it uses a traditional manual film advance, automatic film advance can be achieved with the optional Winder CW.

The Hasselblad 501 C is a medium format film camera that was produced from 1994 to 1997. It is a leaf shutter model within the Hasselblad V-system. The camera was sold in a kit with a Zeiss C Planar f/2.8 80 mm lens.

The Hasselblad 201F is a medium format film camera produced by Hasselblad from 1994 to 1997. It is one of the models compatible with the TTL flash system. It features a focal plane shutter and is compatible with leaf shutter lenses.

The Hasselblad 2000FCW is a 6x6 medium format SLR system camera that was released in 1984. It is an updated version of the 2000FC/M, featuring compatibility with a film winder. This camera marked Hasselblad's return to manufacturing focal-plane shutter-based cameras after more than 20 years. It features an electronic titanium shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/2000 of a second. The 2000FCW has a modular design, allowing for interchangeable lenses, finders, focusing screens, and backs. It is compatible with both F series lenses (without shutters) and C series lenses (with built-in leaf shutters). The camera requires a 6V PX28 battery for operation.

The Hasselblad 500 EL is a medium format film camera introduced in 1965. It is essentially a 500 C with a permanently integrated motor drive in the baseplate, which was a helpful feature for quick shooting due to the 500 C's lack of an instant-return mirror. The camera body includes settings for normal operation, automatic continuous mode at 1 fps, and various speed modes for continuous mirror-up operation. The 500 EL was famously adapted by NASA for the Apollo moon program, with some units remaining on the lunar surface. It was succeeded by the 500 EL/M in 1971.

The Holga 120N is a medium format toy camera known for its simple plastic construction and iconic lo-fi image characteristics, such as soft focus, heavy vignetting, and occasional light leaks. It uses 120 roll film and includes masks for shooting either 6x6cm (12 exposures) or 6x4.5cm (16 exposures) formats per roll. The camera features a fixed 60mm f/8 plastic lens, a zone focusing system that allows focusing from 3 feet to infinity, and selectable aperture settings (f/8 or f/11) for cloudy or sunny conditions. Shutter speed options include a fixed 1/100 second and a bulb mode for long exposures, with film advanced manually using a winding knob and frame count viewed through the rear red window. The body has a standard 1/4-20 tripod mount for stability during long exposure shots and a hot shoe mount for attaching electronic flash units. Designed for ease of use and experimentation, the Holga 120N is widely regarded as a classic among toy cameras, producing distinctive, creative photographs.

The Intrepid 4x5 is a large format film camera that allows photographers to capture stunning, high-resolution images. It features a lightweight and compact design, making it perfect for outdoor photography. The camera is made from high-quality materials, ensuring durability and longevity. It has a bellows system that allows for flexible focusing and perspective control. The Intrepid 4x5 also offers interchangeable lens boards, giving photographers the freedom to use a variety of lenses. With its precise movements and intuitive controls, this camera is a great choice for photographers who want to explore the world of large format photography.

The Intrepid 5x7 is a large format field camera made by Intrepid Camera, a company founded in 2015. This model features an aluminum base and plywood panels, available with black, red, blue, or green bellows. It is part of a range of moderately-priced cameras, with its cost kept low through material choices. The 5x7 model, like other later Intrepid cameras, allows for rear tilt movements.

The Kiev 88 is a medium format film camera that was manufactured in the Soviet Union. It is a clone of the Hasselblad 1600F and offers a similar modular design. The camera features a 6x6cm square format and uses interchangeable lenses and film backs. It has a focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/2s to 1/1000s, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. The Kiev 88 has a waist-level viewfinder for composing images and a built-in light meter for accurate exposure. It is a sturdy and reliable camera, known for its affordability and compatibility with Hasselblad accessories. However, it can be quite heavy and bulky to carry around. Overall, the Kiev 88 is a popular choice among medium format film photographers.

The Kiev 60 is a medium format SLR film camera manufactured by Arsenal Factory in Kiev, Ukraine, from 1984 to 1999. It is a 6x6cm camera that uses 120 roll film and is inspired by the Pentacon Six, sharing the same lens bayonet mount. The Kiev 60 features an interchangeable 80mm f/2.8 Volna-3 MC lens with an automatic diaphragm. It has a curtain-type cloth focal plane shutter with speeds from 2 to 1/1000 seconds, plus a bulb mode. The camera includes an eye-level SLR pentaprism finder, which is interchangeable with a waist-level finder, and a full-aperture TTL CdS cell exposure meter in the prism. The Kiev 60 is known for its affordability and for handling like an oversized 35mm SLR, making it a choice for amateur medium format photography.

The Kiev 4 is a 35mm rangefinder camera produced by Arsenal in Kiev, Ukraine, from 1956 to 1987. It is a development of the Kiev II and III, which were copies of the Contax II and III. The camera features a Contax mount for lenses and a vertical blade shutter with speeds from B to 1/1250. It is known for its long 9 cm rangefinder base, which allows for accurate focusing, and its combined viewfinder and rangefinder window. Some models, like the Kiev 4, include a selenium cell exposure meter, while the Kiev 4A is a non-metered variant.

The Kiev 6S, also known as the Kiev 6C, is a medium format SLR camera produced in Ukraine by the Arsenal factory during the Soviet era. Its design is closely based on the Pentacon Six. This fully manual camera features TTL metering within its removable prism and accepts both 120 and 220 roll film. It utilizes a cloth focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/1000 to 1/2 second, plus a bulb setting. The Kiev 6S uses interchangeable lenses with the Pentacon Six mount. Original lenses for this model were uncoated. A distinguishing feature of the Kiev 6S is its left-hand shutter button.

The Kodak Ektar H35 is a compact 35mm film camera that was produced by Kodak in the 1970s. It features a fixed 35mm f/2.8 lens and a fully automatic exposure system. The camera has a sleek and stylish design with a silver metal body and a black leatherette covering. It has a built-in light meter that helps you determine the correct exposure settings for your photos. The Ektar H35 also has a built-in flash for low-light situations. It uses 35mm film, which is widely available and easy to find. The camera is lightweight and portable, making it perfect for travel and everyday use. Overall, the Kodak Ektar H35 is a reliable and user-friendly film camera that produces high-quality images.

The Kodak Retina III is a 35mm rangefinder camera manufactured by Kodak AG in Germany and introduced in 1954. It uses standard 35mm film and features a coupled rangefinder and viewfinder for precise focusing. The Retina III is equipped with a Synchro-Compur leaf shutter offering speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second, and typically comes with a Schneider-Kreuznach Retina-Xenon 50mm f/2 lens. Notable features include a built-in selenium light meter (in the Retina IIIC and IIIS variants) and interchangeable front lens elements on some models. The camera is known for its compact folding design and high-quality optics. It was part of the well-regarded Retina series, popular among enthusiasts for its portability and performance.

The Kodak Retina IIIc (Type 021 Model I) is a 35mm camera introduced at Photokina Cologne in 1954. It features an f/2 50mm Xenon or Heligon lens and a coupled rangefinder. This model includes an uncoupled exposure meter that reads in Light Values. The Retina IIIc has a Synchro-Compur shutter with speeds from 1 second to 1/500, and its lens assembly slides forward, providing more rigidity than earlier Retina models. It also has a film advance lever on the camera base and supports interchangeable front lens components.
The Kodak Star EF is a 35mm viewfinder camera. It was made in China and features a built-in flash. This model also includes a sliding lens cover.

The Konica Auto S3 is a compact rangefinder camera that was introduced by Konica in 1973. It features a fixed 38mm f/1.8 lens, which provides sharp and bright images. The camera has a built-in light meter that measures the exposure and sets the shutter speed automatically. It also has a manual mode for those who prefer to set the exposure manually. The Auto S3 has a solid and durable construction, with a metal body and a leatherette covering. It has a fast and accurate rangefinder focusing system, which makes it easy to capture sharp images. The camera is known for its excellent image quality and low-light performance. It uses 35mm film and has a motor drive option for continuous shooting. Overall, the Konica Auto S3 is a reliable and versatile camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Konica C35, introduced in 1968 by Konishiroku, is a 35mm compact film camera and the first model in a series that included the C35 V, C35 Automatic, and the Auto S3 (C35 FD). The C35 is notable for pioneering the proliferation of compact cameras in the early 1970s, influencing many subsequent designs from other Japanese manufacturers. It features a compact and lightweight body, a high-quality lens with a wider-than-average angle for the time, a built-in CdS light meter positioned in the lens mount, and a rangefinder for accurate focusing (except on the C35 V and C35 E&L). The camera employs an automatic exposure system, making it accessible and easy to use for general consumers. Three main versions were produced: the original C35 (1968, with silver and black finishes), the non-rangefinder C35 V (1971, known in Japan as the C35 E&L), and the C35 Automatic (1971, also called C35 Flashmatic in Japan) with advanced flash control. The Konica C35 was a global commercial success and set a standard for the compact camera market of its era.

The Konica C35 Automatic (also known as “Flashmatic” in Japan) is a compact 35mm rangefinder film camera introduced in 1971. It features a fixed 38mm f/2.8 lens with a 46mm filter thread and a fully automatic exposure system, making it accessible for users seeking simple point & shoot operation. The camera offers ASA/ISO settings from 25 to 400, a shutter speed range of 1/30 to 1/650 second, and focuses from 1 meter to infinity using its coupled rangefinder mechanism. Construction emphasizes durability with a sturdy metal body, compact form factor, and minimal electronic components, reducing points of failure. The C35 Automatic weighs approximately 380 grams, maintaining portability for everyday use or outdoor activities. Its reputation for reliable performance, combined with reasonable secondhand prices, makes it a practical choice for photographers seeking a straightforward, high-quality film camera without elaborate electronic features.

The Konica C35 Automatic (also known as C35 Flashmatic in Japan) is a compact 35mm rangefinder film camera introduced in 1971. It features a fixed 38mm f/2.8 lens with a 46mm filter thread and a fully automatic exposure system, making it accessible for users seeking simple point & shoot operation. The camera offers ASA/ISO settings from 25 to 400, a shutter speed range of 1/30 to 1/650 second, and focuses from 1 meter to infinity using its coupled rangefinder mechanism. Construction emphasizes durability with a sturdy metal body, compact form factor, and minimal electronic components, reducing points of failure. The C35 Automatic weighs approximately 380 grams, maintaining portability for everyday use or outdoor activities. Its reputation for reliable performance, combined with reasonable secondhand prices, makes it a practical choice for photographers seeking a straightforward, high-quality film camera without elaborate electronic features.

The Konica Hexar AF is a high-end point-and-shoot film camera that was first introduced in 1993. It is known for its sleek design, robust build quality, and advanced features. The camera features a fixed 35mm f/2 lens, which is renowned for its sharpness and low-light performance. It has a built-in motor drive that allows for fast and precise autofocus, making it ideal for capturing quick moments. The Hexar AF also offers various shooting modes, including aperture priority, manual exposure, and program auto. It has a quiet shutter release, which makes it great for street photography. The camera uses 35mm film and has a motorized film advance and rewind system. It also has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure metering. Overall, the Konica Hexar AF is a reliable and versatile camera that is highly sought after by both professional and amateur photographers.

The Konica Hexar RF is a 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Konica in 1999. It is known for its high-quality build, exceptional image quality, and advanced features. The camera features a sleek and compact design, with a black metal body and a comfortable grip. It has a built-in motor drive, which allows for fast and quiet film advance, making it ideal for street photography and capturing candid moments. The Hexar RF has a bright and clear viewfinder with a built-in rangefinder, which makes it easy to focus accurately. It also has an automatic exposure mode, as well as manual exposure control for more creative control. The camera uses interchangeable lenses, and it is compatible with Leica M-mount lenses, making it a versatile choice for photographers. Overall, the Konica Hexar RF is a highly regarded camera that offers a blend of classic design, advanced features, and excellent image quality.

The Konica T4 is a classic 35mm film camera known for its compact and lightweight design. It was first introduced in 1984 as an upgrade to the popular Konica T3. The T4 features a sleek black body with a built-in flash and a fixed 35mm f/3.5 lens. It has a fully automatic exposure system with a range of shutter speeds from 1/8 to 1/500 seconds. The camera also offers a self-timer and a hot shoe for external flash. With its simple operation and reliable performance, the Konica T4 is a great choice for beginners and enthusiasts alike.

The Konica Autoreflex T, introduced in 1968, was the first focal plane shutter 35mm SLR to combine auto-exposure and TTL metering in one body. Known as the FT A in Japan and Revue Autoreflex TTL in Germany, this model marked a shift to a non-hyphenated "Autoreflex" name. It is a fully mechanical camera featuring shutter-priority auto exposure. Its CdS light meter requires two PX 675 type mercury batteries. The camera offers a shutter speed range from 1s to 1/1000s and Bulb. A special version, the Autoreflex W, included a timing back to imprint exposure times on film.

The Konica Autoreflex TC, introduced in 1976, was designed as an entry-level SLR camera, replacing the A3 model. It is a scaled-down, more compact camera compared to earlier Autoreflex models, reflecting a trend in the photographic industry towards smaller SLR cameras. The Autoreflex TC features shutter speeds ranging from 1/8 to 1/1000s, plus a Bulb setting. In Japan, this model was marketed as the Acom-1. While the Acom-1 was offered with a Date Back option in 1978, the Autoreflex TC never included this feature. Both the TC and the T4, a similar but more advanced model, utilized a plastic top plate but retained a metal frame for durability.

The Konica C35 EF, nicknamed "Pikkari" in Japan, is a compact camera introduced in 1974. It was the first 35mm compact camera to feature a built-in electronic flash, accommodating all necessary components within its compact body. The camera is equipped with a Konica Hexanon 38mm f/2.8 lens and utilizes zone focusing by selecting preset distances on the rotating lens barrel. It features auto-exposure via a CdS metering cell and has shutter speeds of 1/60 and 1/125. The integrated auto-flash automatically adjusts aperture based on ambient light and focus distance. Film speed can be manually set from ASA/ISO 25-400. The C35 EF requires a 1.3V PX675 mercury battery for the light meter and two AA alkaline batteries for the flash.

The Kowa Six is a medium format single-lens reflex (SLR) camera produced by Kowa in the 1960s, designed for 6x6 cm exposures on 120 roll film. Unlike many competing models such as the Bronica S2 and Hasselblad, the Kowa Six loads film directly into the body rather than into detachable magazines; the film routes through an L-shaped path inside the camera. The original Kowa Six was later improved as the Kowa Six MM, which added features such as a mirror lock and multiple exposure capability, and then evolved into the Super 66 model with interchangeable film magazines. The system included a range of Kowa lenses and several viewfinder, focusing screen, and accessory options. While the Kowa Six is known for its robust construction and high-quality optics, the mirror movement can cause the focusing ring to shift if not held securely during exposure. Careful operation is recommended to avoid mechanical jams, which can be reset by removing the film and reopening the camera.

The Leica CL is a compact 35mm film rangefinder camera introduced by Leica in 1973. It was designed in collaboration with Minolta, making it the only Leica camera that was not entirely manufactured by Leica. The CL features a Leica M bayonet mount, allowing it to use a wide range of Leica M lenses. It has a built-in light meter and a rangefinder focusing system. The camera has a solid build quality with a metal body and a leatherette covering. It offers full manual control and has a shutter speed range from 1/2 to 1/1000 seconds. The Leica CL is a popular choice among photographers who prefer a compact and lightweight camera with the renowned Leica quality.

The Leica IIIg is a legendary 35mm rangefinder camera produced by Leica from 1957 to 1960. It is the final model in the Leica III series and is highly regarded for its exceptional build quality and precision engineering. The camera features a compact and durable all-metal body, with a top-mounted film advance lever and a collapsible viewfinder. It has a built-in coupled rangefinder that allows for precise focusing, and a cloth focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/1000 to 1 second, plus bulb mode. The IIIg also introduced the use of a built-in exposure meter, making it the first Leica rangefinder to have this feature. The camera uses interchangeable screw-mount lenses and has a wide range of accessories available, including viewfinders, flash units, and motor drives. With its timeless design and exceptional performance, the Leica IIIg remains a sought-after camera for both collectors and photographers.

The Leica M2 is a legendary 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Leica in 1957. It is considered one of the finest film cameras ever made and is highly sought after by photographers and collectors alike. The M2 features a compact and durable all-metal construction, with a precision-crafted metal body and high-quality optics. It has a bright and clear viewfinder with a built-in rangefinder for accurate focusing. The camera uses interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to choose from a wide range of Leica M-mount lenses. The M2 also has a simple and intuitive control layout, with manual focus and exposure settings. It is known for its exceptional image quality, thanks to its high-quality lenses and precise mechanical design. The Leica M2 is a timeless classic that continues to be cherished by photographers who appreciate the art of film photography.

The Leica M3 is a legendary 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Leica in 1954. It is considered one of the most iconic and sought-after cameras in the world of photography. The M3 features a solid and durable construction with a brass top and bottom plate, making it a rugged and reliable camera. It has a bright and clear viewfinder with a combined rangefinder patch for accurate focusing. The camera uses interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to choose from a wide range of Leica M-mount lenses. The M3 also has a unique double-stroke film advance lever, which provides a smooth and precise film winding experience. It offers a wide range of shutter speeds from 1s to 1/1000s, giving photographers full control over exposure. The Leica M3 is highly regarded for its exceptional build quality, precise mechanics, and outstanding image quality.

The Leica M4 is a legendary 35mm rangefinder camera that was produced by Leica from 1966 to 1975. It is considered one of the best cameras ever made and is highly sought after by collectors and photographers alike. The M4 features a compact and robust design, with a top plate made of brass and a body covered in vulcanite. It has a bright and clear viewfinder, allowing for precise focusing and composition. The M4 also has a reliable and accurate light meter, making it easier to achieve proper exposure. Overall, the Leica M4 is a masterpiece of craftsmanship and engineering, offering exceptional image quality and a timeless design.

The Leica M4-P is a 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Leica in 1980. It is an improved version of the Leica M4-2, with added features and enhancements. The M4-P is known for its exceptional build quality and precision engineering, making it a favorite among professional photographers and enthusiasts. It features a bright and accurate viewfinder, which allows for precise focusing and composition. The camera also has a built-in light meter, which helps in getting the correct exposure settings. The M4-P has a durable and robust construction, with a brass top plate and bottom plate. It has a manual film advance lever and a rewind crank, making it easy to load and unload film. The camera is compatible with Leica M-mount lenses, which are renowned for their optical quality. Overall, the Leica M4-P is a reliable and versatile camera that delivers excellent image quality and is a joy to use.

The Leica M5 is a 35mm rangefinder camera produced by Leica from 1971 to 1975. It was the first Leica M camera to feature through-the-lens (TTL) metering, making exposure control more accurate and convenient. The M5 has a solid and robust build, with a durable metal body and a leatherette covering. It uses the Leica M mount, allowing for compatibility with a wide range of Leica lenses. The camera offers a bright and clear viewfinder with a 0.72x magnification, making it easy to focus and compose shots. The M5 also features a built-in light meter, which provides accurate exposure readings for both ambient and flash photography. It has a shutter speed range of 1s to 1/1000s, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. Overall, the Leica M5 is a reliable and versatile camera that is highly regarded by enthusiasts and professionals alike.

The Leica M6 is a legendary 35mm rangefinder camera known for its exceptional build quality and precision. It was introduced in 1984 as the successor to the popular Leica M4-P. The M6 features a compact and robust metal body, making it a reliable companion for photographers. It has a bright and clear viewfinder with a rangefinder mechanism that allows for accurate focusing. The camera offers manual exposure control, allowing photographers to have full creative control over their images. The M6 also has a built-in light meter for convenient exposure metering. It is compatible with Leica M-mount lenses, providing a wide range of lens options for photographers. The Leica M6 is highly regarded for its exceptional image quality and timeless design, making it a favorite among film enthusiasts and professionals.

The Leica M7 is a 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Leica in 2002. It is a manual focus camera that combines the classic design and craftsmanship of Leica with modern features. The M7 features a built-in light meter, which makes it easier to achieve accurate exposures. It also has aperture-priority mode, allowing photographers to set the desired aperture and let the camera automatically adjust the shutter speed. The camera has a durable and compact body, making it ideal for travel and street photography. The M7 uses Leica's M-mount lenses, which are renowned for their exceptional optical quality. Overall, the Leica M7 is a versatile and reliable camera that is highly regarded by photographers for its precision and image quality.

The Leica MP is a 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Leica in 2003. It is an all-mechanical rangefinder focusing camera that follows in a long line of cameras since the Leica M3 was introduced in 1954. The camera uses the Leica M-mount, which accepts all Leica bayonet-mount lenses (21 mm through 135 mm) made since 1954. The 'MP' designation stands for mechanical perfection. Unlike the preceding Leica M7, the camera has adopted many retro design features from the earlier M3. These include a M3 type metal film advance lever, knob film rewind design and M3 type frameline adjust lever. The basic classic design remains unchanged and the design for loading film from the bottom has been retained. The camera comes in black paint or silver chrome finishes.

The Leica R6.2 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Leica in 1992 as an upgraded version of the original R6. It is a manual focus camera that offers a robust and reliable build quality, making it a popular choice among professional photographers. The R6.2 features a bright viewfinder with a 0.72x magnification, allowing for accurate composition and focusing. It has a shutter speed range from 1s to 1/2000s, with a flash sync speed of 1/100s. The camera supports both manual and aperture-priority exposure modes, giving photographers full control over their shots. With its durable construction and precise mechanics, the Leica R6.2 is a reliable tool for capturing high-quality images.

The Leica M-A (Typ 127) is a purely mechanical 35mm rangefinder camera released by Leica Camera AG in 2014. It has no exposure meter, no electronic control, and requires no battery to operate. The camera is Leica's first purely mechanical camera since the Leica M4-P in 1981. Its specifications are similar to the Leica M4-P, with exterior features resembling the Leica M2. The M-A is noticeably slimmer than its digital counterparts and is enclosed in all-metal using chromed brass top and bottom covers. It comes in black or silver chrome finish. The camera allows full manual control and is compatible with M-mount lenses from 16 to 135mm. A lever allows changing framing lines for different lens pairs: 28/90mm, 35/135mm, and 50/75mm.

The Leica M4-2 is a 35mm rangefinder system camera produced by Leica from 1977 to 1983. It is a reintroduction of the M4, manufactured in Canada, with some detail differences and simplified, largely mechanized production. The M4-2 features a Leica M lens mount, a focal plane shutter with speeds from 1/1000 to 1 second, and a reverse Galilean viewfinder with 0.72x magnification. It has a coupled rangefinder for manual focusing and provides manual exposure control. For the first time, provision was made for a motor winder. The camera is all mechanical and does not have a built-in exposure meter. It includes a fixed hotshoe for flash synchronization.

The Leica Minilux is a compact 35mm camera produced by Panasonic for Leica, first introduced in 1995. It features a Leica Summarit 1:2.4/40mm lens with 6 elements in 4 groups. The camera offers shutter speeds from 1 to 1/400 seconds, plus a bulb mode, and has an optical viewfinder with 0.35x magnification. It supports film speeds from ISO 25 to ISO 5000. Exposure modes include program and aperture priority, with center-weighted metering. Focusing is handled by an overrideable active infrared autofocus system. The Minilux has fully automatic film advance and a small top LCD monitor for status display. It is powered by a CR123A lithium battery.

The Leica Mini Zoom is a 35mm compact rangefinder point-and-shoot camera produced in the mid-1990s. It features a Vario Elmar 35-70mm f/4.0-7.6 zoom lens. The camera includes several program modes such as bulb, infinity focus, and exposure override. Its shutter speed range is from 1/4 to 1/300 second. The longest automatic exposure is 1/4 second at f/4.0. In limited light, if the camera cannot use its longest exposure value in manual modes, it resorts to bulb mode. The Mini Zoom was advertised for candid images, but it has a significant shutter lag.

The Linhof Master Technika is a large format film camera that offers exceptional versatility and precision. It is widely regarded as one of the best field cameras ever made. With its compact and lightweight design, it is perfect for outdoor photography and on-location shoots. The camera features a bellows system that allows for extensive movements, including tilt, swing, and shift, giving photographers full control over perspective and focus. The Master Technika supports a wide range of film formats, from 4x5 to 8x10 inches, allowing photographers to capture stunning detail and clarity. Its robust construction ensures durability and reliability, making it a favorite among professional photographers. The Linhof Master Technika is a timeless classic that continues to be cherished by film enthusiasts and photographers who appreciate the art of large format photography.

The Lomography Sprocket Rocket is a 35mm panoramic film camera introduced by Lomography in 2011. It is notable for exposing the entire width of the film, including the sprocket holes, resulting in unique panoramic images. The camera features a 30mm wide-angle lens with a fixed aperture of f/10.8 and two shutter speed settings: 1/100s and bulb mode. Focusing is zone-based, with settings for 0.6m, 1m, and infinity. The Sprocket Rocket includes a rewind knob for multiple exposures and creative film rewinding. Its simple plastic construction and manual controls make it popular for experimental and creative analog photography.

The LOMO LC-A+ is a 35mm compact camera produced by Lomography in 2006, based on the original LOMO LC-A. Manufactured in China, it features improvements over its predecessor, including multiple exposure capabilities, support for film speeds up to 1600 ISO, a cable release compatible shutter button, and front threading for accessories. Early versions of the LC-A+ came with the Russian-made Minitar lens, while models released from 2007 onwards typically featured Chinese-made lenses. The camera has a 3-element 32mm 1:2.8 Minitar lens with a 63-degree angle of view and zone focus settings at 0.8m, 1.5m, 3m, and infinity. It offers shutter speeds from 1/500 to unlimited and an X-synchronized hotshoe mount for flash. The LC-A+ lacks the zone focus markers in the viewfinder and the aperture setting option found in the original LC-A.

The Mamiya 6 is a medium format rangefinder camera that was introduced in 1989. It is known for its compact and lightweight design, making it a popular choice among photographers who value portability. The camera features a collapsible lens system, allowing it to be easily stored and carried. It uses 120 or 220 roll film, which allows for 12 or 24 exposures, respectively. The Mamiya 6 offers interchangeable lenses, providing photographers with versatility in their shooting. It has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure readings and a rangefinder focusing system for precise focusing. The camera also has a variety of exposure modes, including aperture priority, manual, and bulb. Overall, the Mamiya 6 is a reliable and versatile medium format camera that delivers high-quality images.

The Mamiya 645 is a medium format film camera that was first introduced in 1975. It is known for its modular design and versatility, making it a popular choice among professional photographers. The camera features a 6x4.5cm format, which is larger than 35mm but smaller than traditional 6x6cm medium format cameras. It has a built-in light meter and a waist-level viewfinder, as well as interchangeable lenses and film backs. The Mamiya 645 offers excellent image quality and is suitable for a wide range of photography genres, including portrait, landscape, and commercial photography.

The Mamiya 645 Super is a medium format film camera that was introduced in 1985 as an upgrade to the original Mamiya 645. It is a modular system camera that offers versatility and high image quality. The camera features a 6x4.5cm format, which is larger than the standard 35mm format, resulting in sharper and more detailed images. It has a sturdy and ergonomic design, with a comfortable grip and intuitive controls. The Mamiya 645 Super is compatible with a wide range of interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to choose the perfect lens for each situation. It also offers various accessories such as interchangeable viewfinders, motor drives, and backs for different film formats. Overall, the Mamiya 645 Super is a reliable and versatile camera that is well-suited for professional photographers and enthusiasts who value image quality and flexibility.

The Mamiya 7 is a medium format rangefinder camera that was introduced in 1995. It is known for its compact and lightweight design, making it a popular choice among professional photographers who need a portable medium format camera. The Mamiya 7 features a 6x7cm film format, which allows for larger negatives and higher image quality compared to 35mm cameras. It has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control and a bright viewfinder for easy focusing. The camera is compatible with a range of high-quality lenses, offering photographers versatility in their shooting. With its robust construction and reliable performance, the Mamiya 7 is a reliable choice for photographers who value image quality and portability.

The Mamiya 7II is a medium format rangefinder camera known for its exceptional image quality and portability. It features a 6x7cm film format, allowing for larger negatives and higher resolution. The camera is equipped with a built-in light meter and offers manual exposure control, as well as aperture priority and program modes. The Mamiya 7II has interchangeable lenses, providing versatility for different shooting situations. It has a bright and clear viewfinder, making it easy to focus and compose images. The camera is well-built and durable, perfect for professional photographers and enthusiasts who value reliability and image quality.

The Mamiya C220 is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera manufactured by Mamiya and introduced in 1968. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The camera features interchangeable lenses and focusing screens, a unique capability among TLRs. The C220 has a manual film advance with a frame counter and does not have an automatic stop, requiring users to align frame numbers manually. It offers parallax correction and close focusing down to 9 inches (23 cm) with certain lenses. The camera is fully mechanical and does not require batteries for operation.

The Mamiya C3 is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera introduced by Mamiya in 1962. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The camera features interchangeable lens units, making it unique among TLRs, and supports a range of Mamiya Sekor lenses. The C3 has a bellows focusing system, allowing for close-up photography, and a focusing knob with a distance scale. It includes a waist-level viewfinder and accepts interchangeable focusing screens. The Mamiya C3 is notable for its robust build and modular design, catering to both professional and advanced amateur photographers.

The Mamiya C330 is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera that was first introduced in 1969. It is known for its exceptional build quality and versatility, making it a popular choice among professional photographers. The C330 features interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to choose from a wide range of focal lengths to suit their needs. It also has a unique bellows focusing system, which enables close-up and macro photography. The camera has a waist-level viewfinder, which provides a bright and clear image for composing shots. The C330 has a reliable and accurate light meter, making it easy to achieve proper exposure. It uses 120 and 220 roll film, allowing for both square and rectangular formats. Overall, the Mamiya C330 is a reliable and versatile camera that delivers high-quality images.

The Mamiya MSX500 is a 35mm SLR film camera produced by Mamiya in the 1970s. It features a sturdy and durable metal body with a classic black finish. The MSX500 offers a fully manual shooting experience, allowing photographers to have full control over their exposure settings. It has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings. The camera also has a through-the-lens (TTL) metering system, which ensures accurate metering in various lighting conditions. The MSX500 has a reliable and smooth film advance mechanism, making it easy to advance to the next frame. It has a bright and clear viewfinder, making it easy to compose and focus your shots. Overall, the Mamiya MSX500 is a reliable and versatile film camera that is perfect for photographers who prefer manual control and high-quality images.

The Mamiya Press is a system of medium-format rangefinder press cameras produced by Mamiya from 1960 through the 1970s. Designed primarily for professional press photographers, the cameras offered interchangeable lens and back systems, with the original model featuring the M-type back attachment, a 90 mm lens, and rear bellows allowing up to 15 degrees of tilt and 31 mm of extension. The system supported a maximum negative size of 6×9 cm using 120 or 220 rollfilm, with compatibility for various film backs (M-type and G-type), sheet film holders, and Polaroid pack film. Multiple rollfilm holders were available, supporting different formats and frame counts, and focusing aids included a focusing screen, ground glass, and hoods. The rangefinder had a baseline of 60–61.2 mm and magnification of 0.66–0.72×, with later models featuring switchable brightline frames for various focal lengths and automatic parallax correction. Additional accessories included dedicated viewfinders for wide-angle lenses and a sports finder, making the Mamiya Press a flexible and modular camera system for a wide range of professional uses.

The Mamiya RB67 is a medium format, single-lens reflex camera that was first introduced in 1970. It is known for its modular design and exceptional image quality. The RB67 features a large bellows system, allowing for a wide range of lens movements and close-up photography. The camera uses 120 or 220 roll film, providing 6x7cm or 6x4.5cm image formats, respectively. It has a robust build quality, with a metal body and a bright waist-level viewfinder. The RB67 offers interchangeable film backs, lenses, viewfinders, and other accessories, making it highly versatile for various photographic applications. It is widely used by professional photographers and studio shooters for its reliable performance and exceptional image quality.

The Mamiya RB67 Pro SD is a medium format film camera known for its exceptional image quality and versatility. The RB67 Pro SD uses 120 or 220 roll film and produces 6x7cm negatives, providing a larger image area compared to 35mm cameras. The RB67 Pro SD also has a built-in light meter for convenient exposure control. The Mamiya RB67 Pro-S is a medium format film camera that was introduced in 1974 as an upgrade to the original RB67. The RB67 Pro-S also has a built-in motor drive option, enabling rapid film advance and continuous shooting. The Mamiya RZ67 is a medium format film camera known for its exceptional image quality and versatility. It features a modular design, allowing photographers to easily switch between different film backs, viewfinders, and lenses. The RZ67 uses a bellows focusing system, which allows for precise control over depth of field and perspective. With its large negative size of 6x7cm, the RZ67 produces incredibly detailed and sharp images. The camera also offers a wide range of shutter speeds, from 8 seconds to 1/400th of a second, providing flexibility in various shooting conditions. The RZ67 is popular among professional photographers and is often used for studio work, portraiture, and landscape photography.

The Mamiya RZ67 Pro II is a medium format film camera that was released in 1995 as an upgrade to the original RZ67 Pro. It is widely regarded as one of the best professional medium format cameras ever made. The RZ67 Pro II features a modular design, allowing for interchangeable lenses, viewfinders, and film backs. It uses a bellows focusing system, which provides precise control over focus and allows for close-up photography. The camera has a large and bright waist-level viewfinder, as well as a built-in metering system.
