The RZ67 Pro II is known for its exceptional image quality, thanks to its high-quality lenses and the large 6x7cm negative size. It is a favorite among professional photographers for its versatility, durability, and superb image quality.

The Mamiya 23 Standard is a medium-format rangefinder press camera introduced in July 1965 as part of the Mamiya Press system, a lineup designed for professional press photographers. It is a simplified version of previous models, omitting rear bellows but featuring an interchangeable lens mount compatible with the rest of the Mamiya Press line. The camera supports a variety of film formats, with a maximum image size of 6 × 9 cm on 120 or 220 rollfilm, and is compatible with multiple interchangeable film backs, including rollfilm, cut film, and film pack adapters. The Mamiya 23 Standard does not have an internal dark slide, requiring users to insert a slide into the film holder before changing lenses. It uses a reverse Galilean rangefinder with a 0.66× magnification and 60 mm effective baseline length, and various supplementary and sports viewfinders were available as accessories. The camera could also use different focusing aids, such as ground glass backs and focusing hoods, supporting a wide range of professional applications.

The Mamiya Super 23 is a medium-format rangefinder press camera introduced in August 1967 as a major revision to the Mamiya Press series, primarily aimed at professional press photographers. It features a redesigned body and retains a rear bellows system, which allows for swing and shift movements of the film plane, enhancing perspective and focus control. The Super 23 has a large viewfinder with switchable brightlines for 100mm, 150mm, and 250mm lenses, and improved rangefinder precision with 0.72× magnification and a 61.2 mm effective baseline. It uses modular film backs, with compatibility for both M-type and, via an adaptor, G-type back interfaces, supporting a range of formats including 6×9 cm, 6×7 cm, 6×6 cm, and 645, on 120 or 220 rollfilm, as well as pack film and cut sheet film. The standard lens is 100mm, but a variety of lenses and wide-angle finders were available. The system lacks an internal dark slide, requiring external slides to change lenses or backs, and offers multiple focusing aids such as ground glass backs and focusing hoods. Accessories included sports finders and a variety of film holders, making the Super 23 a highly adaptable and modular camera for professional use during its production era.

The Mamiya M645 1000S is a medium format SLR camera that was introduced in 1976. It is an upgrade to the original M645 model, featuring a faster top shutter speed of 1/1000th of a second, a self-timer, and a depth of field preview button. The camera uses 120 or 220 film, offering 15 or 30 exposures respectively. It has an interchangeable finder system, allowing for various prism and waist-level viewfinders, and interchangeable focusing screens. The M645 1000S utilizes a moving coil electronic focal plane shutter and has an instant return, automatic mirror system with mirror lock-up. It is powered by a 6V silver-oxide PX28 battery.

The Mamiya 6 MF is a medium format rangefinder camera that was released in 1993 as a revision of the New Mamiya 6. It is known for its multi-format support, offering 6x6 and 6x4.5 formats with a masking insert, and also accommodating 35mm film with a panoramic adapter for 24x54mm images.

The Mamiya 645 Pro is a medium-format SLR camera introduced in April 1992 by Mamiya in Japan. It makes fifteen 6x4.5 cm images on 120 roll film and features a polycarbonate body. Unlike its predecessor, the 645 Pro lacks a mechanically-timed shutter speed, meaning it requires battery power to operate. It uses the same bayonet lens mount as earlier M645 models, and film inserts are interchangeable. The camera's manual highlights several features, including a 'T' exposure when using the self-timer with the shutter dial set to 'B', and automatic setting of the camera's focal-plane shutter to 1/8 second when using leaf-shutter lenses.

The Mamiya 645 Pro TL is a medium-format SLR camera made in Japan by Mamiya, part of a series that began in the mid-1980s. It makes fifteen 6x4.5 cm images on 120 roll film. Unlike Mamiya's 6x7 SLR cameras, it relies on helical focusing in the lenses rather than bellows. The camera body is made mainly from polycarbonate, a departure from the metal bodies of earlier M645 models. It shares the same bayonet lens mount and interchangeable film inserts with earlier M645 cameras, though viewfinders are not interchangeable between the series. The 645 Pro TL was eventually replaced by the auto-focus 645 AF series from late 1999.

The Mamiya 645E is a medium-format SLR camera made in Japan by Mamiya, introduced in March 2000. It makes fifteen 6x4.5 cm images on 120 roll film. This model is a simplified version of other cameras in its series, featuring a fixed metering prism finder with a Keplerian magnifier/dioptric correction eyepiece and a fixed film chamber that uses film inserts like the original M645. The shutter speed dial is located on the left side of the body, and the hot shoe is on top of the prism. The 645E uses the same bayonet lens mount as earlier Mamiya 645 cameras.

The Mamiya C33 is a medium format Twin Lens Reflex (TLR) camera that was released in 1965 as part of the Mamiya C series. It is an improved version of the Mamiya C3 and features an automatic shutter cocking mechanism during film winding. The camera uses a film advance crank that automatically stops after turning clockwise and requires a counter-clockwise return. It includes a dedicated lens distance scale window on the right side of the body, providing scales for 65mm and 80mm focal lengths, with additional scales on the left side bellows plate for 105mm, 135mm, and 180mm lenses. Some models also have scales for 55mm and 250mm lenses. The lens parallax selection knob on the left side has settings for 80mm, 105mm, 135mm, and 180mm lenses. The C33 primarily uses 120 film, with some variations supporting 220 film backs. It features a proprietary Mamiya covering with a raised 'M' instead of leatherette.

The Mamiya 645 AFD is a medium format SLR camera that was released in December 2001 by Mamiya, following the 645 AF. It is an auto-focus camera and was designed to be compatible with certain digital backs, though these were not produced by Mamiya at the time. This model, along with its successors the 645 AFDII and 645 AFDIII, retains the ability to use either film or a digital back, allowing for quick switching between the two, even mid-roll. The camera features a new bayonet lens mount with electrical contacts to support AF lenses. Unlike the previous M645 Super/Pro series which had polycarbonate bodies, the 645 AF series, including the AFD, features aluminum bodies. Many features from Mamiya's earlier 4.5x6cm SLR cameras are retained, but the 645 AFD is not as modular, with a built-in power film winder and AE prism viewfinder.

The Mamiya Universal Press is a medium format rangefinder camera system introduced in 1969. It is a revision of the Mamiya Super 23, featuring a similar body but with the ability to use Mamiya, Graflex, and Land Polaroid backs. This was achieved through a native Press back that accepted P-adapters for M-Type (Mamiya) or G-Type (Graflex) film holders. Unlike the Super 23, it eliminated the rear bellows device. A similar model, the Polaroid 600SE, was marketed, though its lens and film back mounts were not interchangeable with Mamiya models. The Mamiya Universal Press was available in silver and black.

The Mamiya ZM is a 35mm camera released in October 1982. It was the last Mamiya 35mm camera produced. Designed by Tsuneaki Munakata, it is an advanced version of the ZE-2, incorporating some features from the ZE-X. The ZM has an aperture-priority automatic time control, which is based on center-weighted TTL readings. It features a metal electronically controlled automatic shutter-speed range from four seconds to 1/1000, and a manual range from two seconds to 1/1000, plus Bulb mode. The camera is powered by two 1.5v LR44/SR44 coin-type batteries.

The Minolta Autocord series is a line of twin-lens reflex (TLR) medium-format cameras produced by Chiyoda Kogaku Seiko (later Minolta) between 1955 and 1966, designed to compete in the premium TLR market. All Autocords feature a crank film advance mechanism with automatic shutter cocking and frame counting, a four-element Tessar-type Rokkor 75mm f/3.5 lens, slow shutter speeds down to 1 second, and an override for intentional double exposures. The series includes both meterless models and versions with built-in light meters, using either selenium or later CdS cells, and many have an EV number scale or unique 'LVS' exposure value setting system. The cameras are also notable for their underside focus lever, which offers ergonomic advantages over traditional knob-focusing mechanisms, though the lever is susceptible to breakage. Late models, such as the Minolta Autocord I, II, and III, introduced features like 220 film compatibility, adjustable exposure counters, and several metered variants (Autocord CDS, CDS II, CDS III) with expanded ISO settings and battery checks. The Autocord series offered advanced features and high-quality optics at a lower price compared to German competitors like the Rolleiflex, making them significant in the history of Japanese TLR cameras.

The Minolta CLE is a compact 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1980. It was designed in collaboration with Leica and shares the same M-mount as Leica cameras. The CLE features aperture-priority automatic exposure mode, manual exposure mode, and TTL metering. It has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings. The camera has a shutter speed range of 1/1000 to 4 seconds and supports exposure compensation. It has a bright and clear viewfinder with a rangefinder focusing system. The CLE is compatible with a wide range of M-mount lenses, making it a versatile choice for photographers. It is known for its compact size, lightweight design, and excellent build quality.

The Minolta Dynax 7Xi is a 35mm autofocus single-lens reflex (SLR) camera introduced in 1991. It is notable for its innovative automatic functions, including eye-start operation, where the camera begins focusing and can automatically zoom when the photographer brings the camera to their eye. The camera supports Minolta’s program-card system, allowing users to insert pre-programmed chip cards for optimized settings in different shooting scenarios such as landscape, portrait, or sports photography. It also offers full manual control with Program, Aperture priority (A), Shutter priority (S), and Manual (M) exposure modes, and is compatible with all Minolta/Sony A-mount lenses. The 7Xi features a wide range of specifications, including shutter speeds from 30 seconds to 1/8000 second, wireless and built-in pop-up flash with a guide number of 12, multiple metering options, motorized film advance and rewind, and DX-coded ISO setting. The camera operates on a 2CR5 battery and weighs approximately 650 grams.

The Minolta Dynax 800si is a high-performance autofocus SLR camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1997. It is part of the popular Dynax/Maxxum series and is known for its advanced features and excellent build quality. The camera features a durable metal body with ergonomic design, making it comfortable to hold and operate. It has a 35mm film format and supports both manual and autofocus modes. The autofocus system is fast and accurate, allowing for sharp and precise focus in various shooting conditions. The camera also has a built-in motor drive, enabling continuous shooting at up to 4 frames per second. It offers a wide range of exposure modes, including program, aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual. The exposure metering system is highly reliable and provides accurate exposure readings. The Dynax 800si has a large and bright viewfinder, making it easy to compose and frame shots. It also has a built-in flash and supports external flash units for more advanced lighting options. Overall, the Minolta Dynax 800si is a versatile and reliable camera that is suitable for both amateur and professional photographers.

The Minolta Hi-Matic 7sII is a compact rangefinder camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1977. It is the successor to the popular Hi-Matic 7s and offers several improvements and new features. The camera features a sharp 40mm f/1.7 lens, which provides excellent image quality and low-light performance. It has a built-in light meter that helps you accurately expose your photos, and the exposure can be manually adjusted using the aperture and shutter speed controls. The camera has a range of shutter speeds from 1/4 to 1/500 second, allowing you to capture fast-moving subjects or long-exposure shots. The Hi-Matic 7sII also has a built-in self-timer and a hot shoe for attaching an external flash. With its compact size and reliable performance, the Minolta Hi-Matic 7sII is a great choice for both beginner and experienced photographers.

The Minolta Hi-Matic AF was introduced in 1979. It was a step towards the modern standard compact camera for film, not yet with automatic film transport, automatic film speed setting and display. But it already offered active infrared autofocus combined with automatic exposure with speed/aperture-settings between f2.8 + 1/8 sec. to f17 + 1/430 sec. This exposure program is replaced by automatic aperture setting when the flash is switched on. Four LEDs in the bright-frame finder show the distance set by the AF. The CdS exposure measuring window is within the filter thread. The camera has a mechanical self-timer. It needs two AA batteries.

The Minolta Hi-Matic AF2 was the first viewfinder camera for 35mm film with active infrared autofocus when it was launched in 1981 as successor of the Hi-Matic AF. It was one of the last of Minolta's long-lasting Hi-Matic series of quality viewfinder and rangefinder cameras with automatic exposure. In addition to its autofocus the camera has a buzzer which indicates too small object distance or low light. The built-in flash needs two AA-batteries. The camera has the same kind of lens as most other 1970s Hi-Matics, a four-element construction with focal length 38mm. It has also the typical CdS-meter window inside the filter-thread in the front of the lens barrel. Even the film speed selector around the lens is typical 1970s Hi-Matic design, as well as film advance lever and rewind knurl.

The Minolta Maxxum 7000, also known as the Minolta α-7000, is a groundbreaking 35mm autofocus SLR camera that was introduced in 1985. It was the first camera to feature both integrated autofocus and motorized film advance, setting a new standard for SLR cameras. The Maxxum 7000 has a sleek and compact design, with a comfortable grip and intuitive controls. It features a TTL phase detection autofocus system, which allows for fast and accurate focusing. The camera also has a built-in motor drive, enabling continuous shooting at up to 2 frames per second. The Maxxum 7000 offers a wide range of exposure modes, including program, aperture priority, shutter priority, and manual. It has a versatile metering system that combines center-weighted and spot metering for accurate exposure in various lighting conditions. The camera is compatible with a wide range of Minolta A-mount lenses, giving photographers plenty of options for different types of photography. Overall, the Minolta Maxxum 7000 is a reliable and innovative camera that revolutionized the world of autofocus SLRs.

The Minolta Maxxum HTSi+ is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera introduced by Minolta in 1998. It uses the Minolta A-mount lens system and is compatible with a wide range of autofocus and manual focus lenses. The camera features fully automatic, program, aperture-priority, shutter-priority, and manual exposure modes. It includes built-in TTL flash, a top shutter speed of 1/2000 sec, and supports DX-coded film for automatic ISO setting. The HTSi+ offers a user-friendly interface with an LCD display and multiple drive modes, including single, continuous, and self-timer. Notable for its lightweight polycarbonate body, it was marketed as an entry-level SLR for amateur photographers.

The Minolta SR-7 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera introduced by Minolta in 1962. It features a fully mechanical, horizontal-travel cloth focal plane shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/1000 second plus Bulb. The SR-7 was notable for being the first SLR to incorporate a built-in CdS light meter, powered by a mercury battery, with a match-needle system visible in the viewfinder. It uses the Minolta SR bayonet lens mount, supporting a wide range of interchangeable lenses. The camera does not have automatic exposure or a built-in motor drive, relying entirely on manual operation. Its robust, all-metal construction and reliable mechanics made it a popular choice among enthusiasts of its era.

The Minolta SRT 200 is a classic 35mm film SLR camera that was first introduced in 1975. It is part of Minolta's SRT series, known for their robust build quality and reliable performance. The SRT 200 features a rugged metal body with a comfortable grip, making it easy to handle and operate. It has a bright and clear viewfinder, allowing for precise composition and focusing. The camera offers manual exposure control, with a wide range of shutter speeds from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. The SRT 200 has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings, ensuring well-exposed images. It is compatible with a wide range of Minolta MD mount lenses, giving photographers the flexibility to choose the right lens for their needs. Overall, the Minolta SRT 200 is a reliable and versatile camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Minolta SRT-101 is a classic 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera that was introduced in 1966. It was the first camera in the SRT series and quickly became popular among photography enthusiasts. The SRT-101 features a rugged and durable metal body, making it suitable for both amateur and professional use. It has a manual focus system with a bright viewfinder, allowing for precise composition and focusing. The camera offers a wide range of shutter speeds from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. It has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings, and the user can adjust the aperture and shutter speed accordingly. The SRT-101 uses a standard M42 screw mount, which allows for compatibility with a wide range of lenses. Overall, the Minolta SRT-101 is a reliable and versatile camera that is highly regarded for its excellent build quality and performance.

The Minolta SRT201 is a manual focus 35mm SLR camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1975. It is part of the popular SRT series of cameras and is known for its rugged build quality and reliable performance. The SRT201 features a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings, making it easy to achieve well-exposed photos. It has a vertically-traveling metal focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. The camera has a bright viewfinder with a split-image focusing aid and microprism collar, making it easy to achieve sharp focus. It is compatible with a wide range of Minolta MD mount lenses, allowing photographers to explore different focal lengths and creative possibilities. The SRT201 is powered by a standard 1.5V battery and has a self-timer for capturing self-portraits or group shots. With its solid construction and reliable performance, the Minolta SRT201 is a great choice for photographers who prefer the simplicity and control of manual SLR cameras.

The Minolta TC-1 is a compact 35mm film camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1996. It is renowned for its exceptional image quality and compact size, making it a popular choice among professional photographers and enthusiasts. The TC-1 features a fixed 28mm f/3.5 lens, which is known for its sharpness and wide-angle perspective. The camera offers both automatic and manual exposure modes, allowing photographers to have full control over their shots. It also has a built-in flash for low-light situations. The TC-1 is constructed with a durable metal body and has a sleek, minimalist design. It is a highly sought-after camera due to its superb optics and portability.

The Minolta S-1 was designed to be splashproof by using a porro mirror optical viewfinder, rather than the typical SLR pentaprism. The camera features a compact design, owing to the use of mirrors instead of prisms in the viewfinder. It is equipped with three basic autoexposure modes (Program, Aperture-priority, Shutter-priority) and Manual exposure modes. The standard metering pattern is a 14-segment honeycomb pattern covering the central part of the frame, but the camera can be switched to spot metering mode. The S-1 supports mid-roll changes.

Like the S-1, the Minolta S-100 is weather resistant to light rain and snowy conditions. Compared to the S-1, the S-100 is equipped with a simpler exposure meter (two-segment, no spot metering option) and shutter (fastest speed reduced to 1⁄1000 s and flash synchronization speed slowed to 1⁄90 s). In addition, the optical viewfinder has slightly less coverage of the final frame area. It offers the same exposure modes (PASM) and subject-specific program exposure modes, and also uses a central autofocus sensor. The camera features a compact design, owing to the use of mirrors instead of prisms in the viewfinder.

The Minolta X-370s is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1981. It is a manual focus camera with aperture-priority and manual exposure modes. The X-370s features a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings for a wide range of lighting conditions. It has a metal chassis and a durable construction, making it a reliable camera for both amateurs and professionals. The camera has a vertical-travel, metal-blade focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. It has a bright viewfinder with a split-image focusing screen and a microprism collar, making it easy to achieve precise focus. The X-370s is compatible with a wide range of Minolta MD mount lenses, allowing photographers to explore different focal lengths and creative possibilities. Overall, the Minolta X-370s is a versatile and dependable camera that offers excellent image quality and control.

The Minolta X-570 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1983. It is part of the popular X series of cameras and is known for its reliable performance and advanced features. The X-570 features a fully automatic exposure mode, as well as aperture priority and manual exposure modes. It has a bright viewfinder with a split-image focusing screen and a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control. The camera has a durable metal body and a comfortable grip, making it easy to handle and carry. It uses Minolta's MD lens mount, allowing for a wide range of compatible lenses. The X-570 is a versatile camera that is suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Minolta X-700 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1981. It is widely regarded as one of the best manual focus SLRs ever made. The X-700 features a fully mechanical shutter with speeds from 1s to 1/1000s, as well as an aperture priority auto-exposure mode. It has a TTL metering system with center-weighted average metering and a range of -1 to 20 EV. The camera has a bright and clear viewfinder with a split-image focusing aid and a microprism collar. It also has a self-timer and a multiple exposure function. The X-700 is compatible with a wide range of Minolta MD lenses and accessories, making it a versatile choice for photographers. It is highly regarded for its build quality, reliability, and ease of use.

The Minolta XD5, is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1975. It is the little brother to the xd7. The XD-5 was stripped of a couple of minor features (aperture readout, film transport check) but retains most of the functionality, most importantly the electronically-controlled Seiko shutter and the innovative multimode adaptive metering. This camera gives the choice between aperature priority and shutter speed priority by providing both.

The Minolta XD7, also known as the Minolta XD11 in the North American market, is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1977. It was part of the popular XD series and was known for its advanced features and solid build quality. The XD7 featured a vertically-traveling focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, as well as a fully manual exposure mode and aperture priority and program modes. It had a bright viewfinder with a split-image focusing screen and a built-in light meter that provided accurate exposure readings. The XD7 also had a self-timer, depth-of-field preview, and multiple exposure capability. It was compatible with a wide range of Minolta MD lenses, allowing photographers to explore different focal lengths and creative possibilities. The XD7 was highly regarded for its reliability and performance, making it a popular choice among both amateur and professional photographers.

The Minolta XD-s is a 35mm SLR film camera manufactured by Minolta and introduced in 1979. It is a variant of the Minolta XD series, closely related to the Minolta XD-7 (XD11 in North America), and was primarily released for the Japanese domestic market. The XD-s features both aperture-priority and shutter-priority automatic exposure modes, as well as full manual control. It uses the Minolta SR mount for interchangeable lenses and offers a bright viewfinder with LED exposure indicators. Notable features include a depth-of-field preview, multiple exposure capability, and a smooth electromagnetic shutter release. The camera is powered by two SR44 or LR44 batteries and is known for its compact, robust design.

The Minolta XE-7 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Minolta in 1974. It is part of the X series of cameras and is known for its robust build quality and advanced features. The XE-7 features a metal body with a comfortable grip, making it easy to handle and carry. It has a bright viewfinder with a split-image focusing screen, allowing for precise manual focusing. The camera has a vertical-travel, metal-blade focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. It also has an exposure compensation dial and a self-timer function. The XE-7 is compatible with a wide range of Minolta MD lenses, giving photographers plenty of options for different shooting situations. Overall, the Minolta XE-7 is a reliable and versatile camera that is well-suited for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Minolta XG-1 is a 35mm SLR film camera introduced by Minolta in 1977. It uses the Minolta SR bayonet lens mount, compatible with a wide range of Minolta manual focus lenses. The camera features aperture-priority automatic exposure as well as full manual exposure control. Shutter speeds range from 1/1000 to 1 second, plus Bulb mode, and it uses a horizontal cloth focal plane shutter. The XG-1 includes through-the-lens (TTL) center-weighted metering and an electronically controlled shutter, requiring batteries for operation. Notable features include a hot shoe for flash, self-timer, and a bright viewfinder with LED exposure indicators.

The Minolta X-300 is a 35mm manual focus SLR camera produced by Minolta between 1984 and 1990, also marketed as the X-370 in the U.S. and Canada. It features an electronically-controlled cloth-curtain focal plane shutter with manual speeds from 1 to 1/1000 second, and stepless speeds up to four seconds in aperture-priority mode. The camera has a center-weighted average light meter mounted in the pentaprism, a 10-second self-timer, and AE lock. It supports an ISO range of 12-3200 and uses two AG13/LR44 batteries. The X-300 was a less expensive alternative to the X-500, with a nearly identical body but fewer features, such as the absence of OTF flash mode, a DOF preview button, PC connection, and interchangeable screens. It became the basis for many other cameras from China after Minolta's autofocus Maxxum line was introduced.

The Minolta Dynax 5, also known as Maxxum 5 in the Americas, α-Sweet II in Japan, and α-5 in China, is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera introduced around 2002. It features an electronically controlled vertical-travel focal-plane shutter with speeds from 30 seconds to 1/4000 second, plus bulb mode, and a flash sync of 1/125 second. The exposure system uses a 14-segment honeycomb silicon photo diode for TTL metering, offering a range of 1 to 20 EV, and includes PASM modes (Program, Aperture priority, Shutter priority, Manual), along with scene modes. It has a built-in auto pop-up flash with a guide number of 12. The TTL autofocus system has a range of -1 to 18 EV, with single or continuous modes and an AF illuminator. The camera supports DX-coded film from 25 to 5000 ISO, with manual settings from 6 to 6400 ISO. It features motorized film transport with single or continuous advance up to 3 frames per second, automatic and mid-roll manual rewinding, and an eye-start feature that automatically sets exposure and focus when the camera is brought to the eye. The Dynax 5 is powered by two CR2 batteries.

The Minolta XG-M, introduced in 1981, was the flagship model of the Minolta XG series of 35mm SLRs. It featured a completely new design and was available in chrome only, replacing the XG 9 in its markets. The Japanese version was known as the X-70. The XG-M corrected a major limitation of earlier XG models by allowing the light meter to function in manual exposure mode. It included all the features of the XG-S, such as a stop-down button and the brighter "Acute Matte" focusing screen. The ASA setting and exposure adjustment were moved to the rewind crank, and it could be mounted on the 3.5-fps Motor Drive 1.

The Leica CL is a 35mm compact rangefinder camera with interchangeable M-mount lenses, developed in collaboration with Minolta, who also manufactured it. It was first released in April 1973, with a Japanese market version, the Leitz Minolta CL, appearing in November 1973. Both versions were produced in a Minolta factory in Osaka. The camera features a vertical-running focal plane shutter with cloth curtains, offering speeds from ½ to 1/1000 second. It includes a through-the-lens CdS exposure meter mounted on a pivoting arm, similar to the Leica M5, and provides manual exposure with a mechanical shutter. Shutter speeds are visible in the viewfinder, which has framelines for 40mm, 50mm, and 90mm lenses. The CL was sold with specially designed Leitz Summicron-C 40mm f:2 and Leitz Elmar-C 90mm f:4 lenses, which were also branded as Minolta M-Rokkor lenses for the Leitz Minolta CL. It is known for its compact size and affordability as a platform for M-mount lenses, though its rangefinder is less precise than those of Leica M bodies.

The Minolta Dynax 9 is an autofocus 35mm SLR camera produced by Minolta around 1999. It was also marketed as the Maxxum 9 in the USA and the Alpha 9 (α-9) in Japan. This model succeeded the 9xi and 800si and features a Minolta A-type bayonet lens mount. The camera is known for its robust construction, including rubberized and weatherproof controls. A rare variant, the Dynax 9Ti, was later released with a titanium body. The Dynax 9 shares similar controls with the 600si. It is equipped with a focal plane shutter offering speeds from 30 seconds to 1/12000 second, with flash synchronization at 1/300 second, and includes a built-in flash. The Minolta α-9 received the Japan Camera Grand Prix award in 1999.

The Minolta XG 7, also known as the XG-E in some markets, was the first model in the Minolta XG series of 35mm SLRs, introduced in 1977. This series was designed as a budget-friendly line of small, lightweight, and easy-to-use electronic SLRs with an automatic exposure mode. The XG 7 features a center-weighted metering system with two CdS cells and a matte-fresnel-field focusing screen with a horizontal split-image spot. Its viewfinder displays automatic shutter times from 1s to 1/1000s via LEDs. It is considerably smaller and lighter than Minolta's preceding cameras and was available in both chrome and black finishes.

The Minolta Dynax 500si Super is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera produced by Minolta around 1995. It was also marketed as the Maxxum 500si in the American market, and as the Maxxum 530si RZ and Maxxum 550si with additional features. The Japanese version was known as the α-303si Super. It features an electronically controlled focal-plane shutter with speeds from 30 seconds to 1/2000 second and a flash sync of 1/90. The camera offers five program exposure modes, including portrait, landscape, close-up, sport, and night portrait. Its TTL metering system uses an 8-segment honeycomb silicon photocell with a range of 1 to 20 EV, and it supports DX-encoded films from 25 to 5000 ISO. Film transport is motorized, with single or continuous drive up to 1fps, and automatic or manual rewind. It includes a built-in flash with a guide number of 12 and an AF illuminator for low-light focusing. The camera is powered by a 2CR5 battery.

The Minolta Dynax 505si, also known as the Maxxum HTsi Plus, is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera body released in 1998. Compared with the later Dynax 505si Super, it lacks Eye Start focus and the film leader out custom function, and limits multiple exposures to two. The camera features a plastic lens mount, reducing its weight by 25g. It was the first Minolta SLR to combine a central cross autofocus sensor with two vertically placed sensors. The Dynax 505si offers five programmed modes, a fully automatic mode, shutter-preferred, aperture-preferred, and manual modes. It has a shutter speed range from 30 seconds to 1/4000 second, a built-in flash with a guide number of 12.

The Minolta Dynax 9xi, also known as the Maxxum 9xi or α-9xi, was Minolta's flagship 35mm film SLR from its third generation of autofocus system cameras. Introduced in the early 1990s, it featured a data setting thumb wheel near the shutter release and an LCD display under the focusing screen for exposure manipulation. Designed for professionals, particularly in sports photography, it boasted a fast focal plane shutter capable of 4.5 frames per second and speeds up to 1/12000 second, with a maximum flash sync of 1/300 second. Its intelligent autofocus system could predict movements in three dimensions, powered by a 16-bit 20MHz microprocessor utilizing "fuzzy logic" algorithms with data from a 14-field metering sensor. The camera also supported an image lock mode for series photography with automatic zoom adjustment and was compatible with the new Minolta 5400xi system flash, which could be remote-controlled for TTL flash photography. Special chip cards were available to simplify the use of its advanced features.

The Minolta SR-T 102 is a 35mm SLR camera that is essentially a Minolta SR-T 101 with several enhancements. It features a hot shoe for flash synchronization, a focusing screen equipped with a split-image rangefinder for precise focusing, and the capability for multiple exposures. Additionally, the selected aperture value is visible within the viewfinder, providing convenient exposure information to the photographer. This model was known as the SR-T Super in some markets and the SR-T 303 in others.

The Minolta XE-5 is a 35mm SLR camera introduced in 1975, positioned as a less advanced sibling to the Minolta XE series, and was not sold in the Japanese home market. It features a fixed finder, a vertical-running metal blade shutter, and a bright viewfinder with an exposure meter scale for both manual and automatic operation. The camera offers meter-assisted manual or aperture-priority automatic exposure settings. Its electronically controlled shutter provides speeds from 4 seconds to 1/1000 second, with a mechanical backup speed of 1/90 second and Bulb. Standard features include a hot-shoe, a self-timer, and a PC X sync contact. The XE-5 operates on a 3V silver battery or two 1.5V SR44 batteries, and it typically comes with an MC Rokkor-X PF 1:1.7 f=50mm lens. The camera's prism housing is entirely black, distinguishing it from other models in the series.

The Minox 35 GT-X is a compact 35mm film camera that was introduced by Minox in 1981. It is part of the Minox 35 series, known for their small size and high-quality optics. The GT-X features a fixed 35mm f/2.8 lens, which produces sharp and detailed images. It has a fully automatic exposure system, with a built-in light meter that measures the ambient light and sets the aperture and shutter speed accordingly. The camera also has a manual override option, allowing the user to adjust the exposure settings manually. The GT-X has a range of shutter speeds from 1/500 to 30 seconds, making it suitable for various shooting conditions. It has a built-in flash, with both automatic and manual flash modes. The camera has a sturdy metal body and a compact design, making it easy to carry around. Overall, the Minox 35 GT-X is a reliable and versatile camera that delivers excellent image quality in a compact package.

The Nikon EL2 is a 35mm SLR camera introduced in 1977, notable for its electronically-controlled shutter and aperture-priority automatic exposure function. As the successor to the Nikkormat ELW, it was among Nikon’s first cameras to support AI (Automatic Indexing) lenses, utilizing a modern F-mount and a silicon photo-diode (SPD) light meter for more accurate metering. The EL2 features a fixed prism and a fixed focus screen, and provides electronic shutter speeds from 1/1,000 to 8 seconds, as well as a mechanical 1/90 second speed for shooting without a battery (PX28 type). It offers exposure modes including manual and aperture-priority AUTO, with a full analog needle display in the viewfinder for metering and settings information. Additional key features include a wide ASA range, exposure compensation dial, auto-exposure lock, and compatibility with the AW-1 winder. The Nikon EL2 was discontinued in favor of the Nikon FE in 1978, but remains a significant bridge between Nikon’s earlier mechanical SLRs and more modern electronic models, highlighting advancements such as improved metering, AI lens compatibility, and enhanced user ergonomics.

The Nikon EM is a 35mm film SLR camera introduced by Nikon in 1979. It features aperture-priority automatic exposure with a mechanical backup shutter speed of 1/90 second. The camera uses Nikon's F-mount, allowing compatibility with a wide range of Nikkor lenses. The EM has a vertical-travel, electronically controlled metal focal-plane shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/1000 second plus Bulb. It includes a through-the-lens (TTL) center-weighted metering system and a hot shoe for flash. Notably compact and lightweight, the Nikon EM was designed as an entry-level SLR for amateur photographers.

The Nikon F is a legendary 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1959. It was the first SLR camera to feature interchangeable lenses and a modular design, allowing photographers to customize and adapt the camera to their specific needs. The Nikon F quickly became popular among professional photographers and photojournalists for its robust build quality, reliable performance, and wide range of available lenses and accessories. It features a focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, a bright and clear viewfinder, and a durable metal body. The Nikon F has a reputation for being a workhorse camera that can withstand harsh conditions and deliver exceptional image quality. It is still highly regarded by film enthusiasts and collectors today.

The Nikon F100 is a professional-level 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced in 1999. It is part of Nikon's F series, which has a long history of delivering high-quality cameras. The F100 is known for its advanced features and exceptional performance, making it a popular choice among professional photographers. It features a durable and ergonomic design, with a rugged metal body and comfortable grip. The camera has a fast and accurate autofocus system, with 5 autofocus points and 3D matrix metering for precise exposure control. The Nikon N2020, also known as the Nikon F501, is a 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1986. The Nikon F6 is a professional 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced in 2004. It is the successor to the popular Nikon F5. The Nikon F60, also known as the N60 in North America, is a 35mm autofocus SLR film camera introduced by Nikon in 1998. The Nikon N6006, also known as the F601 in some markets, is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1990. The Nikon F65 (N65 in the U.S.) is a 35mm film SLR camera introduced by Nikon in 2001, targeting the lower end of the amateur autofocus market. A variant model, the F65D, included date/time imprinting functionality.

The Nikon F80, also known as the Nikon N80 is some markets, is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Nikon in 2000. The Nikon F90, also known as the Nikon N90 in some markets, is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera released by Nikon in 1992. The Nikon FA is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1983. It is known for its advanced features and versatility, making it a popular choice among professional photographers. The Nikon FE is a 35mm SLR camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1978. It is part of Nikon's compact F-series cameras and is known for its reliability and versatility. The Nikon FE2 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1983 as an upgraded version of the popular Nikon FE. The Nikon FG is a 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1982. It is a compact and lightweight camera that is perfect for beginners and intermediate photographers. The Nikon FG-20 is a compact and lightweight 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1984. The Nikon FM is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera introduced by Nikon in 1977. Metering is handled by a center-weighted, match-needle system powered by two SR44 or LR44 batteries, but the camera remains fully functional without batteries except for the meter. The FM is known for its robust, all-metal construction and manual exposure control, making it popular among enthusiasts and professionals. Notable features include a depth-of-field preview button, mirror lock-up, and a self-timer.

The Nikon FM2 is a 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1982 as an advanced successor to the popular Nikon FM. The Nikon FM3A is a manual focus 35mm film SLR camera that was introduced by Nikon in 2001. The Nikon L35AF is a compact 35mm point-and-shoot film camera introduced in the 1983, notable for being Nikon’s first autofocus camera. The Nikkormat EL is a 35mm SLR film camera manufactured by Nikon and introduced in 1972. The Nikkormat EL is powered by a single 6V PX28 or equivalent battery, which is required for all shutter speeds except the mechanical backup speed of 1/90 second and Bulb. Notable features include a depth-of-field preview button, mirror lock-up, and a hot shoe for flash synchronization.

The Nikon One Touch AF35, also known as the Nikon L35AF2, is a 35mm compact autofocus camera introduced by Nikon in 1985. The Nikon One Touch AF35 is recognized for its reliability and ease of use, making it popular among casual photographers.

The Nikon S2 is a 35mm rangefinder camera produced by Nikon from 1954 to 1957. It is the successor to the Nikon S and features several improvements. The Nikon S3 is a classic rangefinder camera that was introduced by Nikon in 1958. It was part of the Nikon S series, which was known for its high-quality construction and precision optics. The Nikon SP is a professional 35mm rangefinder camera manufactured by Nikon and introduced in 1957. It uses standard 35mm film and features a focal plane shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/1000 second plus bulb. The camera is notable for its advanced viewfinder system, which includes a parallax-corrected main finder with selectable bright-line frames for six different focal lengths. The Nikon SP offers interchangeable lenses via the Nikon S-mount and supports a wide range of Nikkor lenses. It also features a self-timer, flash synchronization, and a robust all-metal construction. The SP is regarded as one of the most advanced and versatile rangefinder cameras of its era.

The Nikon F75, also known as the N75 in North America and U2 in Japan, is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera released by Nikon in 2003. It was one of the last consumer 35mm autofocus SLRs marketed by Nikon and was available in both silver and black finishes. The F75 was discontinued in 2006. This camera was the replacement for the F65. The F75 can only use DX coded film, setting non-DX film at 100 ISO, and infrared films cannot be used. It features a prewind film transport system, where the entire roll is offloaded onto the take-up spool upon loading and then wound back into the canister as film advances after exposure. This system ensures that exposed shots are not ruined if the camera back is opened. The camera counts down the number of available shots. Power is supplied by two CR2 batteries.

The Nikon 35Ti is a compact camera introduced in 1993, featuring a 35mm f/2.8 Nikkor lens. It utilizes an infrared autofocus system, with manual focus also available. The camera includes a built-in electronic flash and offers various operational modes selected via switches and buttons. Its construction incorporates a titanium body, providing both lightness and durability. The 35Ti employs matrix metering and offers exposure compensation. It also provides a cropped panorama mode for 35mm film and a Quartz Date function. A distinctive feature is the top-mounted window displaying four analog scales with "clock hands" to indicate exposure number, aperture, distance, and under/over-exposure compensation. The camera is powered by a 3V CR123A lithium battery.

The Nikon F-801, known as the Nikon N8008 in the USA, is a 35mm film SLR autofocus electronic camera manufactured by Nikon Corporation in Japan between 1988 and 1991. It features both autofocus and manual focus modes with an electronic rangefinder, utilizing a TTL phase detection system (Nikon Advanced AM200 module). The camera is equipped with an electromagnetically controlled vertical-travel focal-plane metal shutter, offering speeds from 30 to 1/8000 seconds plus Bulb. It supports multiple exposure modes including programmed auto-multi, shutter priority auto, aperture priority auto, and manual. The F-801 incorporates matrix metering and center-weighted metering, with a film speed range of 6-6400 ASA. Its body includes a fixed eyelevel SLR pentaprism viewfinder and an LCD panel displaying various settings. An updated version, the F-801S (N8008S), was released in 1991 with improved focusing and spot metering.

The Nikon FM10 is a 35mm SLR camera introduced by Nikon in 1995. It is a manual focus, manual film transport model, manufactured by Cosina and derived from the Cosina CT1 Super. The FM10 accepts Nikon F-mount lenses and features a vertically moving metal focal plane shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/2000 second, plus Bulb. It includes a TTL center-weighted full aperture exposure measuring system with a metering range of EV2-19. The camera also offers a mechanical self-timer, multiple exposure option, and a depth-of-field preview lever. Its viewfinder covers 92% of the field of view and has a magnification of 0.84X. The FM10 was designed as an amateur model and remained on the market into 2015 due to its back-to-basics appeal for traditionalists and students of film photography.

The Nikkormat FTN is a 35mm SLR camera introduced in 1967 by Nippon Kōgaku, and was a successful iteration of the Nikkormat FT series. It is built on the same chassis as the FT but features center-weighted metering instead of whole-frame average metering, a shutter-speed display in the viewfinder, and a simplified lens mounting process. The FTN was produced until 1976 and represents the most common of the FT series Nikkormats. It improved upon its predecessor's user experience by replacing the fully-manual lens indexing with a simpler film speed setting and a "double twist" method for attaching the lens, which automatically indexes the aperture. The Nikkormat series was Nikon's budget range, taking F-mount lenses, and the FTN was considered an update rather than a new model.

The Nikon F55, known as the N55 in the United States, is an entry-level 35mm film SLR camera first released in 2002. This lightweight, mostly-plastic autofocus camera offers P/S/A/M exposure modes. It provides full autofocus and metering capabilities with G-type lenses, and is compatible with screw-type AF and AF-D lenses, though AF lenses without D default to non-3D matrix metering. It does not support autofocus with AF-S and AF-I lenses, nor does it meter with most manual-focus lenses, except for AI-P lenses. The F55 features a built-in flash with TTL metering, but external flashes do not offer this function. It lacks a depth of field preview button and manual ISO setting, automatically setting non-DX coded film to ISO 100. A notable feature is its reverse film loading mechanism, where the entire roll is spooled onto the take-up reel upon loading and rewound into the canister as photos are taken, preventing accidental exposure of already-shot frames if the camera back is opened. The camera is powered by two CR2 batteries, with date back variations also using a CR2025 coin battery. Production of the F55 ceased in 2006.

The Nikon F70, also known as the N70 in the US, is a 35mm SLR camera with autofocus, introduced by Nikon in 1994. It features an electronic shutter with speeds ranging from 1/4000 to 30 seconds, plus a Bulb setting, and offers matrix, center-weighted, and spot metering modes. The camera has a built-in TTL flash and a motorized film transport capable of advancing film at up to 3.7 frames per second in high continuous mode. Its interface is characterized by an unusual design that requires holding buttons on one side while operating a thumb dial on the opposite side, with settings displayed on a circular LCD screen. The F70 is compatible with Nikon F-mount lenses, with full functionality for AF, AF-D, AF-S, and AF-I lenses, and partial compatibility with AI, AI-S, and G lenses.

The Nikon AF600, also known as the Lite•Touch AF, is an autofocus, auto-exposure, compact camera for 35mm film, introduced by Nikon in 1993. At the time of its introduction, it was the world's smallest and lightest AF/AE camera. It features a fixed 28mm f/3.5 wide-angle lens, composed of 3 elements in 3 groups, with an aperture range of f/16 to f/3.5 and a focus distance from 0.35m to infinity. The lens has an automatic cover that opens and closes with power cycling. The camera offers a panorama mode, which captures images at 12.3 x 36 mm, and a self-timer with a two-shot mode. It is compatible with DX-encoded films at 100, 200, 400, and 1000 ISO, with non-coded film set to 100 ISO.

The Nikon F50, known as the N50 in the United States, is an entry-level 35mm film SLR camera introduced by Nikon in 1994. It features autofocus, Through-the-lens light metering, and various program modes ranging from manual operation to a highly-automated point-and-shoot mode. The F50 body is constructed from polycarbonate and metal, and was available in both "champagne silver" and black. A variant, the F50D/N50D, included a date/time-imprinting facility and a panoramic mode. The camera utilizes a Nikon F mount and an electronically controlled vertical-travel focal-plane shutter with speeds from 1/2000 to 30 seconds. It supports ISO 25 to 5000 for DX coded film and ISO 6 to 6400 for non-DX coded films in Advanced mode. The F50 was replaced by the F60/N60 in 1998.

The Nikkormat FT, known as the Nikomat FT in Japan, was introduced in 1965. This original Nikkormat body features averaging metering, similar to the Nikon F Photomic T. Its viewfinder does not display the shutter speed, and the meter needle brackets are thin without "+" and "-" markings. The meter requires manual indexing against the film speed. The FT was later superseded by the FTN.

The Nikon 28Ti is a 135 film autofocus camera released in 1994, distinguished by its 28mm f/2.8 Nikkor lens and titanium body. Its most notable feature is the analog display on the top, which uses four needle-style dials to show focusing distance, aperture, frame number, and exposure correction. This allows users to operate the camera from the waist. The camera features a seven-element blade shutter with speeds ranging from 2 seconds to 1/500 second, which are automatically selected by the exposure modes. The 28Ti was designed as a premium, easy-to-transport offering for photography enthusiasts, though it was discontinued in 1998 due to poor sales.

The Nikon F90X, known as the N90s in the United States, is a 35mm autofocus SLR camera introduced in 1994 and discontinued in 2001. It uses Nikon's F lens mount and was designed for advanced amateur photographers. Key features include a bright viewfinder with 92% coverage, a top LCD display for settings, and an ASA range of 6-6400 with DX-enabled film reading. It offers shutter speeds up to 1/8000 second, various exposure modes including program, aperture-priority, and shutter-priority, and 3D Matrix metering. The F90X is compatible with nearly all Nikkor F-mount lenses and SB series speedlights, and it was also used as the base for the Kodak DCS 400 series of digital SLRs.

The Nikon F-301, introduced in 1985, is a manual focus 35mm SLR camera with motorized film advance and an automatic programmed exposure system controlled by TTL metering. Known as the N2000 in the US market, it was Nikon's first SLR without a film advance lever and featured easy-load, motorized film transport for continuous shooting up to 2.5 fps. It was also the first Nikon camera with DX recognition for film speeds and the first with polycarbonate construction. The F-301 offers shutter speeds from 1 to 1/2000 second, as well as P/PHi and A modes where speeds are electronically controlled. It uses TTL metering for compatible flashes and an electronic shutter release cable. Film rewind is manual, with a lever that also incorporates an ISO selector and exposure compensation dial.

The Nikonos I, introduced in 1963, was the world’s first commercially successful amphibious 35mm film camera, developed from the French Calypso. It featured a watertight die-cast body using O-ring seals, making it water-resistant down to 50 meters, and suitable for both underwater and all-weather land use. The camera used a proprietary Nikonos bayonet lens mount and was paired with specially designed optics, including a 35mm f/2.5 lens usable in air and underwater, and an underwater-specific 28mm f/3.5 lens. The shutter offered speeds from Bulb up to 1/500 second, with a combined lever for film advance and shutter cocking. Compact and relatively lightweight at about 700g with lens, it was far more convenient than previous housing-based designs and quickly gained popularity with divers, researchers, and professionals working in harsh environments. The Nikonos I set the standard for future amphibious cameras and was produced until 1968.

The Nikonos II, released in 1968, was an improved version of the original. Major changes included a switch from a rewind knob to a retractable crank for easier and quicker film rewinding, as well as the introduction of a hinged, pop-up film pressure plate for more convenient film loading. The camera retained the basic watertight, O-ring-sealed design and depth rating to 50 meters, as well as the same lens mount and shutter configuration as the Nikonos I. The viewfinder, shutter speeds, and overall internal layout were mostly unchanged, though the body shape was slightly streamlined. The addition of the “II” logotype next to the viewfinder marked this version. It weighed about 655g with lens, and offered improved handling, making it popular among both amateur and professional underwater photographers.

The Nikonos III, released in 1975, saw several significant operational enhancements. It introduced a film advance sprocket, which standardized the frame spacing throughout a film roll, and moved the frame counter to the top of the body for easier visibility. The viewfinder was upgraded to an illuminating window-type bright frame, offering a clearer, brighter viewing experience and providing additional frame lines for the optional 80mm lens. The hinged pressure plate was further improved, and key controls like the film advance lever, rewind crank, and shutter release button were made larger for easier use with gloved hands. The external appearance, while keeping the spindle shape, became closer to a box-form to accommodate these upgrades. The Nikonos III maintained the 50m depth rating, the Nikonos bayonet lens mount, and a robust, all-weather construction favored by scientific and recreational users alike.

The Nikonos IV-A, introduced in 1980, represented Nikon's first complete redesign of the line, departing from the original Calypso blueprint. Notably, it featured aperture-priority automatic exposure (AE) with through-the-lens (TTL) center-weighted metering, thanks to a reflector in front of the shutter and a silicon photo diode sensor. The electronically controlled shutter offered automatic speeds from 1/30 to 1/1000 sec, with a backup mechanical speed of 1/90 sec and Bulb mode for battery failure contingencies. The camera introduced a hinged, buckle-type camera back for easier film loading, as well as a conventional shutter release button and improved user ergonomics, bringing its operation closer to that of land-based cameras. The IV-A supported dedicated underwater flash systems with TTL compatibility, maintained a 50m depth rating, and weighed about 900g with standard lens. It made underwater photography more accessible through automation and user-friendly controls.

The Nikonos V, launched in 1984, further advanced the series' automation and versatility by adding a manual exposure mode alongside aperture-priority AE. This model featured TTL metered, electronically controlled shutter speeds from 1/30 to 1/1000 sec in auto mode, and manual shutter speeds up to 1/1000 sec, plus a mechanical 1/90 sec speed and Bulb setting. TTL flash metering was introduced for compatible Speedlight models, improving underwater flash photography with automatic exposure control. The camera featured a robust, ergonomically enhanced body available in orange or green, with a hinged camera back and improved sealing against the elements. The Nikonos V retained compatibility with all previous Nikonos lenses, supported ISO films from 25 to 1600, and maintained the 50m depth rating. Its combination of reliability, automation, and compatibility made it the definitive model of the Nikonos series, serving underwater and harsh environment photographers for nearly two decades.

The Nikonos RS AF, released by Nikon in 1992, was the world’s first underwater autofocus single-lens reflex (SLR) camera, marking a significant advancement in underwater photography technology. Built to operate at depths up to 100 meters, the RS AF featured TTL autofocus via Nikon’s AM200 autofocus module, matrix metering for exposure, and both aperture-priority automatic exposure and fully manual modes—capabilities similar to contemporary land-based SLRs. The camera used a proprietary R-UW lens mount and was supported by a dedicated line of underwater-corrected autofocus lenses, including macro, wide-angle, zoom, and fisheye options. Additional features included motorized film advance and rewind, a high eye-point viewfinder optimized for use with dive masks, and compatibility with the SB-104 Speedlight designed for balanced TTL flash exposure underwater. The body and accessories were styled by famed designer Giorgetto Giugiaro and emphasized ergonomic, simplified operation suitable for demanding underwater environments. While technologically advanced, the RS AF was costly and complex to manufacture, resulting in limited production from 1992 until its discontinuation in 1996.

The Noble Design ND 6x17 Pro is a super lightweight 3D printed medium format film camera that weighs only 1035 grams (2.28 pounds) complete with lens, making it roughly half the weight of comparable cameras like the Fuji GX617. The camera is manufactured using HP's Multi Jet Fusion (MJF) 3D printing process and features a sophisticated helical focusing mount with adjustable focus scale ring for critical sharpness with wide-angle large format lenses. It uses an innovative smartphone viewfinder system where users attach their phone to compose shots, take exposure readings, and record reference photos through a dedicated app. The camera is compatible with Super Angulon 90mm F8 and Nikon Nikkor 90mm F8 wide-angle lenses and includes a precision helical focusing mount, adjustable phone clip, and focusing screen. Available as either a body-only kit or with pre-fitted and calibrated lens, the cameras are made to order with approximately 2-3 week shipping times. This represents a modern approach to panoramic medium format photography, combining traditional film capture with contemporary smartphone technology and 3D printing manufacturing.

The Olympus 35 RC is a 35mm rangefinder camera produced in Japan during the 1970s. It features a fixed E. Zuiko 42mm f/2.8 lens with five elements in four groups and supports manual focusing from 0.9 meters to infinity. The camera offers a range of shutter speeds from Bulb (B), 1/15 to 1/500 second, and aperture settings from f/2.8 to f/22. Exposure modes include metered shutter-priority automatic exposure, manual override, and flashmatic modes for versatility. Notably, the 35 RC provides user viewfinder readouts for aperture and shutter speed settings, which was uncommon among compact cameras of its era. The camera accommodates 43.5mm filters, accepts film with ASA ratings between 25 and 800, and weighs 410 grams with compact dimensions of 11 × 7 × 5 cm.

The Olympus 35 RD is a 35mm rangefinder camera produced by Olympus in Japan during the 1970s. It features a fixed 40mm F. Zuiko f/1.7 lens, constructed with 6 elements, and offers manual focusing from 0.85 meters (2.8 feet) to infinity. The camera supports a range of shutter speeds from Bulb, 1/2 second up to 1/500 second, and apertures from f/1.7 to f/16. Exposure can be set using a metered, shutter-priority automatic mode, or via full manual override; in automatic mode, the shutter will not fire if there is not enough light for a proper exposure. The Olympus 35 RD accepts 49mm filters and supports film speeds from ASA 25 to 800. Its compact body measures 11.4 x 7 x 5.7 cm and weighs 482 grams.

The Olympus 35 SP is a classic 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Olympus in 1969. It is known for its high-quality optics and robust build. The camera features a fixed Zuiko 42mm f/1.7 lens, which produces sharp and contrasty images. The lens is coupled with a rangefinder focusing system, allowing for precise and accurate focusing. The camera also has a built-in light meter, which provides accurate exposure readings. It offers both manual and automatic exposure modes, giving photographers flexibility in different shooting conditions. The Olympus 35 SP is a popular choice among film enthusiasts and collectors due to its excellent image quality and reliable performance.

The Olympus AF-1, released in 1986 and also known as the Infinity (US) or “Nurepika” (Japan), is notable for being the world’s first weatherproof, fully automatic 35mm compact camera. Manufactured in Japan, it features a 35mm f/2.8 Zuiko lens with four elements in four groups, autofocus with a ‘focus lock’ option, and fully automatic film loading, advancing, and rewinding. Its built-in automatic flash is powered by a CR-P2 lithium battery and has a recycling time of approximately 1–1.5 seconds. Additional features include a 12-second electronic self-timer, automatic exposure with shutter speeds ranging from 1/30 to 1/750 seconds, and a sliding lens cover for protection. Weighing approximately 225g without battery, the AF-1 stands out for its ease of use, making it popular among both beginners and experienced photographers seeking convenience. Its robust weatherproof design and reliable lens contribute to consistently sharp images with balanced tones, making the Olympus AF-1 a significant model in the history of point-and-shoot film cameras.

The Olympus AF-10 Super is a fully automatic compact 35mm point-and-shoot film camera introduced in the late 1980s, designed for ease of use and basic snapshot photography. Equipped with a 35mm f/3.5 lens and active infrared autofocus, the AF-10 Super delivers reasonably sharp images and is capable of focusing even in low-light conditions. The camera's exposure system is limited, offering automated metering within a narrow range (EV9 to EV15 at ISO 100) by varying shutter speed (1/45s to 1/400s) and aperture (f/3.5 to f/9.1), with no manual override. Flash operation is also automatic, though there are workarounds to make it manual, and only minimal additional user controls are provided (self-timer and a basic viewfinder indicator). Film speed is read via DX coding up to ISO 800, and the camera defaults to ISO 50 when codes are absent, allowing for some creative manipulation with higher-speed films. Its straightforward operation, combined with basic construction and features, make it accessible for beginners, while its predictable shutter speed and simple design can be exploited for creative experimentation by knowledgeable users.

The Olympus Infinity Twin is a 35mm compact film camera introduced by Olympus in 1988. It features a unique dual-lens system, offering both a 35mm f/3.5 wide-angle lens and a 70mm f/6.3 telephoto lens, which can be switched at the press of a button. The camera is fully automatic, with autofocus, auto exposure, and built-in motorized film advance and rewind. It includes a built-in flash with red-eye reduction and a self-timer function. The Infinity Twin is notable for its weather-resistant design, making it suitable for outdoor use. It uses standard 35mm film and is powered by a CR123A lithium battery.

The Olympus Infinity Zoom is a 35mm compact point-and-shoot film camera produced by Olympus, first introduced in the late 1980s. It features a built-in zoom lens, typically a 35-70mm f/3.5-6.6, providing versatility for various shooting situations. The camera is fully automatic, offering autofocus, auto exposure, and motorized film advance and rewind. It includes a built-in flash with red-eye reduction and several flash modes. The Infinity Zoom is known for its weather-resistant body, making it suitable for outdoor use. Its compact design and ease of use made it popular among casual photographers.

The Olympus MJU I, also known as the Olympus Stylus, is a compact 35mm film camera that was first introduced in 1991. It is renowned for its sleek design and weatherproof construction, making it a popular choice for outdoor photography. The camera features a fixed 35mm f/3.5 lens, which offers a wide-angle perspective suitable for landscape and street photography. It also has autofocus capabilities, ensuring sharp and accurate focus in various shooting conditions. The MJU I has a built-in flash with red-eye reduction and auto-exposure control, allowing for easy indoor and low-light photography. With its compact size and user-friendly operation, the Olympus MJU I is a versatile and reliable camera for both beginners and experienced photographers.

The Olympus MJU II, also known as the Stylus Epic, is a compact 35mm film camera that was first introduced in 1997. It quickly gained popularity for its sleek design, high-quality lens, and advanced features. The camera features a 35mm f/2.8 lens, which provides sharp and vibrant images. It has a built-in flash with red-eye reduction and various shooting modes, including landscape, portrait, and night scene. The MJU II also has an autofocus system that ensures quick and accurate focusing. With its compact size and weatherproof construction, it is perfect for travel and outdoor photography. The camera is powered by a CR123A lithium battery, which provides long-lasting power. Overall, the Olympus MJU II is a reliable and versatile camera that delivers excellent image quality in a compact package.

The Olympus OM-1 is a classic 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced in 1972. It is known for its compact size, lightweight design, and exceptional build quality. The OM-1 features a fully mechanical shutter, which means it can operate without batteries, making it a reliable choice for photographers. It has a manual focus system with a bright and clear viewfinder, allowing for precise focusing. The camera has a wide range of shutter speeds from 1 second to 1/1000th of a second, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. The OM-1 uses interchangeable lenses, providing versatility for different types of photography. It is highly regarded by film enthusiasts for its outstanding image quality and ease of use.

The Olympus OM-1n is a fully mechanical 35mm SLR camera produced between 1979 and 1987, and is the final revision of the original OM-1 series. Designed by Yoshihisa Maitani, it features a compact, lightweight body with through-the-lens (TTL) metering and Olympus’s proprietary OM lens mount. Shutter speeds range from Bulb to 1/1000s, with settings located on the lens barrel rather than the top plate, and the camera includes a large, bright viewfinder with a needle-based light meter powered by a single 1.35V battery. The OM-1n added compatibility with a motor drive, improved flash functionality, and included a mirror lock-up feature for long exposures. As a system camera, it supports a wide range of lenses and accessories, including a removable hot shoe and interchangeable focusing screens. While batteries are only needed for metering, the camera remains fully operational without them, making it popular among photographers who prefer a fully manual shooting experience.

The Olympus OM-10 is a 35mm SLR camera that was introduced in 1979. It is part of the Olympus OM series, which was known for its compact and lightweight design. The OM-10 features a manual exposure mode as well as an aperture-priority automatic exposure mode, making it suitable for both beginner and advanced photographers. It has a built-in light meter that provides accurate exposure readings. The camera uses interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to choose the lens that best suits their needs. The OM-10 also has a self-timer and a hot shoe for attaching an external flash. Overall, the Olympus OM-10 is a reliable and versatile camera that is perfect for photographers of all skill levels.

The Olympus OM-2 is a professional 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera manufactured in Japan by Olympus between 1975 and 1988. Building on the earlier OM-1 body, the OM-2 introduced aperture-priority automatic exposure in addition to full manual operation, while maintaining compatibility with all OM-1 lenses and accessories. The OM-2 is notable for being the first camera to feature through-the-lens (TTL) off-the-film direct metering, known as Auto Dynamic Metering (ADM), which enabled precise exposure control, especially with flash photography. The camera used a horizontal-running cloth shutter with auto-exposure times from 60s to 1/1000s (up to 120s on the OM-2N) and a metered manual range of 1s to 1/1000s plus Bulb mode. Several models were produced, including the OM-2, OM-2 MD, OM-2N MD (available in chrome or black finishes), and the OM-2S/OM-2 Spot Program (black only), the latter featuring extensive internal revisions. The OM-2’s innovative metering technology, compact design, and system flexibility established its place as an influential camera among professionals and enthusiasts.

The Olympus OM-2n is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Olympus in 1979. It is part of the Olympus OM system, which was known for its compact and lightweight design. The OM-2n features a fully automatic exposure mode, as well as manual exposure control for advanced photographers. It has a built-in light meter that measures the light through the lens (TTL metering) for accurate exposure. The camera has a vertical metal focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1 to 1/1000 seconds, and it supports multiple exposure and mirror lock-up. The OM-2n has a bright viewfinder with a 0.92x magnification and a split-image focusing screen, making it easy to compose and focus your shots. It uses interchangeable lenses, allowing you to choose the perfect lens for each photographic situation. The OM-2n is a reliable and versatile camera that is loved by both amateur and professional photographers.

The Olympus OM-3 is a professional 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) film camera manufactured in Japan by Olympus Optical Co., Ltd. from 1983 to 1986. It is a fully manual camera, featuring a mechanical shutter and lacking automatic exposure modes. Key innovations include its advanced multi-spot metering system, which supplements traditional center-weighted metering and allows users to take multiple individual spot meter readings for more precise exposure control; this system is operated via a liquid crystal display and includes dedicated highlight and shadow buttons. Additional features of the OM-3 include a maximum shutter speed of 1/2000 second and a built-in flash hot shoe. The OM-3 was produced in smaller numbers compared to its electronic counterpart, the OM-4, and was discontinued after a relatively short production period. In 1995, Olympus introduced the OM-3Ti, an upgraded version with a titanium body, which remained in production until 2002.

The Olympus OM-4 is a 35mm SLR film camera that was introduced by Olympus in 1983. It is part of the highly regarded OM series of cameras, known for their compact size and excellent build quality. The OM-4 features a full manual exposure control, as well as aperture-priority and program modes. It has a built-in light meter that uses a unique multi-spot system, which allows for precise metering even in challenging lighting conditions. The camera has a rugged metal body with a comfortable grip, making it easy to handle and carry. It also has a bright and clear viewfinder, with a split-image focusing screen and a microprism collar for accurate focusing. The OM-4 is compatible with a wide range of Olympus OM lenses, making it a versatile choice for photographers. Overall, the Olympus OM-4 is a reliable and high-performing camera that is well-suited for both beginners and advanced photographers.

The Olympus OM-40 Program is a 35mm film SLR camera introduced in the early 1980s, designed for amateur photographers seeking automated exposure control. The camera features Olympus's ESP (Electro-Selective Pattern) metering system alongside traditional TTL center-weighted metering, offering enhanced exposure accuracy in challenging lighting conditions. It provides three exposure modes: Program (fully automatic), Aperture Priority Auto, and Manual, with shutter speeds ranging from 2 seconds to 1/1000 second plus Bulb mode. The OM-40 supports both DX-coded automatic film speed setting (ISO 25-3200) and manual film speed adjustment, and includes exposure compensation of ±2 EV in 1/3 stop increments. The camera features a pentaprism viewfinder with 93% coverage, electronic self-timer, and compatibility with Olympus OM mount lenses and T-series flash units for OTF (off-the-film) automatic flash control. The body weighs 460g and is powered by two SR44 or LR44 batteries.

The Olympus Pen EE, introduced in 1961, is a compact half-frame 35mm camera notable for its distinctive selenium meter window encircling the lens. Designed for amateur photographers, it features fully automatic exposure and a fixed-focus 28mm f/3.5 lens, making it a true point-and-shoot model. The first version offered a single shutter speed of 1/60 sec, while later revisions provided two speeds (1/200 and 1/40 sec), with the aperture range of f/3.5 to f/22 and ISO settings from 10 to 200. Early models used leatherette cladding, while later versions adopted a characteristic gray basket-weave cover. The camera supports both 22.5mm and 43.5mm filters and was engineered for simplicity, requiring users only to frame and shoot. The Pen EE inaugurated a line of similar models—including the Pen EE-S, EE-D, EE-2, EES-2, EE-3, and EF—each adding features such as improved lenses, focusing ability, easier film loading, expanded ISO ranges, hot shoes, and built-in flash in later generations.

The Olympus PEN F is a vintage 35mm film camera that was first introduced in 1963. It is a half-frame camera, meaning that it captures two images on a single frame of film, resulting in 72 exposures from a standard 36-exposure roll. The PEN F features a compact and lightweight design, making it ideal for street photography and travel. It has a built-in light meter for accurate exposure control and a range of interchangeable lenses, allowing photographers to capture a variety of subjects. The camera also offers manual focus and manual exposure settings, giving photographers full control over their images. With its timeless design and reliable performance, the Olympus PEN F is a popular choice among film photography enthusiasts.

The Olympus Pen FT is a half-frame 35mm SLR camera introduced in 1966 as part of the Pen F series, designed by Yoshihisa Maitani who also created the OM-1 and XA cameras. This mechanical camera produces 18x24mm portrait-format frames on standard 35mm film, yielding 72 exposures per roll instead of the typical 36. The camera features a unique rotary shutter system with speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second and flash sync at all speeds, along with a side-moving mirror mechanism that eliminates the need for a pentaprism, resulting in a compact, flat design. It incorporates an uncoupled Through-the-Lens (TTL) CdS meter powered by a 1.35v battery, with a match-needle system displaying exposure values from 0-7 rather than traditional f-stops. The camera uses a proprietary bayonet mount system for its range of F.Zuiko lenses, which span from 20mm to 800mm focal lengths. The Pen FT was preceded by the original Pen F (1963) and followed by the Pen FV (1967), establishing the first half-frame SLR camera line in photographic history.

The Olympus Stylus Zoom is a classic 35mm point-and-shoot camera first introduced in 1993 and manufactured throughout the 1990s, with over two million units produced. The camera features fully automatic operation including autofocus, automatic exposure control, and automatic aperture selection, making it designed for ease of use. It includes practical features such as a built-in flash, self-timer, tripod mount, and a water-resistant shell for durability. The camera uses a variable zoom lens, with different models offering maximum zoom ranges from 70mm and upward, though all variants share similar form and function.
