Metering operation requires two LR44 (or equivalent 1.5V) batteries, but otherwise, the camera is fully mechanical and can operate without batteries if the meter is not needed. Due to its extended production run, the camera is widely available and remains a popular option for both collectors and those learning manual film photography.

The Yashica Mat-124G is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera that was produced by Yashica from 1970 to 1986. It is a highly regarded camera among photographers and is known for its exceptional build quality and image quality. The Mat-124G features a 6x6cm square format, which is popular among portrait and landscape photographers. It has a fixed 80mm f/3.5 lens with a maximum aperture of f/22. The camera has a waist-level viewfinder, which allows for precise composition and focusing. It also has a built-in light meter for easy exposure control. The Mat-124G is a fully manual camera, giving photographers complete control over their settings. It uses 120 roll film, which provides 12 exposures per roll. The camera has a sturdy metal body and a comfortable leatherette grip, making it a pleasure to hold and use. Overall, the Yashica Mat-124G is a reliable and versatile camera that is well-suited for both amateur and professional photographers.

The Yashica T4 is a compact autofocus point-and-shoot camera that was first released in 1990. It is known for its high-quality Carl Zeiss T* Tessar 35mm f/3.5 lens, which produces sharp and vibrant images. The camera features a built-in flash and a 5-element lens design, allowing for excellent image quality and clarity. It has a maximum shutter speed of 1/700th of a second and a minimum focusing distance of 0.35m. The T4 also has a motorized film advance and rewind system, making it easy to use and convenient for capturing moments on the go. With its sleek design and reliable performance, the Yashica T4 is a popular choice among film enthusiasts and street photographers.

The Yashica T5 is a compact 35mm film camera known for its exceptional image quality and ease of use. It features a high-quality Carl Zeiss T* Tessar 35mm f/3.5 lens, which delivers sharp and detailed images with excellent contrast. The camera has a fully automatic exposure system, making it suitable for both beginners and experienced photographers. It also offers a built-in flash with red-eye reduction and multiple shooting modes, including a self-timer and a continuous shooting mode. The Yashica T5 has a sleek and stylish design, with a durable metal body and a comfortable grip. It is powered by a single CR123A battery, which provides long-lasting performance. Overall, the Yashica T5 is a reliable and versatile camera that delivers impressive results.

The Yashica-D is a twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera that is part of Yashica's knob-wind series of 6x6cm cameras. This model is considered to have more advanced shutters and controls compared to many other knob-wind Yashica TLRs, which often feature more basic shutters and lenses. The Yashica-D, along with the Yashica 635, holds a more intermediate place in the lineup, offering features comparable to some Rolleicord models. All knob-wind Yashica TLRs, including the D, feature front-standard focusing operated by a wheel on the side of the body.

The Yashica Mat-124 is a twin-lens reflex camera produced by Yashica until 1970. It maintains many characteristics of the Yashica-24 and Yashica-12, but uniquely allows selection between 12 and 24 exposures by adjusting the film-pressure plate. This model features a four-element, 80mm f/3.5 Yashinon taking lens and a Copal SV shutter with speeds from 1 to 1/500 second, plus Bulb mode. It includes a self-timer and flash sync for both electronic X and bulb M modes. Focusing is achieved via a ground glass screen with a 3x diopter loupe and a sports finder. The Mat-124 also has a coupled match-needle exposure meter.

The Yashica-A is a 6x6cm twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera that uses 120 roll film. It is one of the knob-wind models in Yashica's line of TLR cameras, which were produced as a budget option compared to their crank-advance counterparts. The Yashica-A typically features a basic shutter with a maximum speed of 1/300s, and it does not include a built-in light meter or thumbwheels. It utilizes front-standard focusing, operated by a wheel on the side of the camera body. This model is known for its simplicity and is considered a basic TLR.

The Yashica-Mat is a 6x6 twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera released by Yashica in 1957. It was the first Yashica TLR to feature crank advance, distinguishing it from earlier models that used knob advance. The camera was branded "Yashica Mat" to indicate its automatic film advance, in contrast to simpler cameras that relied on a red window. Early models were equipped with a 75mm f/3.5 Lumaxar taking lens and a 75mm f/3.2 Lumaxar viewing lens, which were later succeeded by 80mm lenses with the same specifications. The Lumaxar lens, a four-element Tessar-type design, was subsequently renamed Yashinon. The Yashica-Mat utilized either a Copal MX or Copal MXV shutter, offering speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second. Shutter speeds and aperture settings are adjusted via wheels on the front plate, with the cable release employing a "Leica nipple" style.

The Yashica-C is a 6x6cm twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera that is part of Yashica's knob-wind series of cameras. These models were designed as a budget line, retaining many features of the earliest Yashica models. The Yashica-C, like most knob-wind models, features a basic shutter with a maximum speed of 1/300s, lacks a thumbwheel and a built-in meter, and uses fairly basic Tessar lenses. It utilizes front-standard focusing, operated by a wheel on the side of the camera body.

The Yashica T3, also known as the Kyocera T Scope, is a 35mm compact camera from Kyocera. It features autofocus, auto-exposure, and an integrated flash. This model is equipped with a Carl Zeiss T* (coated) 35mm f/2.8 lens, which is faster than other lenses in the T series. A notable feature is its viewing window, or "New Angle Scope," located on the top of the camera body, allowing for waist-level viewing.

The Yashica FX-1 is a 35mm film, mechanically operated, single-lens reflex camera introduced in 1975. It was the first Yashica SLR to feature the Contax/Yashica common bayonet mount, allowing it to use both Yashica and Contax/Carl Zeiss T* lenses. This camera has a horizontal traveling electronic focal plane cloth shutter, offering speeds from 2 seconds to 1/1000 second in auto mode, and 1 second to 1/1000 second plus Bulb in manual mode. It incorporates a CdS light meter powered by a 6V PX28 battery, with a sensitivity range of 0 to 18 EV and an ASA range of 12 to 3200. The viewfinder includes a micro prism spot for focusing, a match needle shutter display, and an aperture display. The film advance lever supports multiple smaller strokes.

The Yashica-Mat LM is a twin-lens reflex camera introduced by Yashica in 1958. The "LM" in its name signifies "Light Meter," referring to the uncoupled selenium cell light meter positioned in front of the viewfinder, which does not require a battery. This camera is entirely mechanical and is noted for its robust construction and ease of use. It utilizes 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm images. The Yashica-Mat LM features an 80mm f/3.5 Yashinon taking lens and a Copal shutter offering speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second, plus Bulb mode, with flash synchronization at all speeds. The viewing lens is a 3.2 Yashinon. Both lenses accept Bayonet I filters. The camera has a metal body covered in black leather, weighs approximately 1.2 kg, and uses a crank for film advance and shutter cocking. The focusing screen includes a Fresnel lens with a red grid and a magnifying loupe for precise focusing.

The Zeiss Ikon Contaflex is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera produced by Zeiss Ikon from 1953 to 1971. It was one of the first SLR cameras to feature an interchangeable lens system. The Contaflex had a sturdy and compact design, making it a popular choice for photographers who wanted a reliable and portable camera. It featured a built-in light meter and a leaf shutter, which allowed for precise exposure control. The camera had a focal plane shutter with speeds ranging from 1/2 to 1/500 seconds, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. The Contaflex was compatible with a wide range of high-quality Zeiss lenses, offering photographers versatility in their shooting. Overall, the Zeiss Ikon Contaflex was a well-built and versatile camera that appealed to both amateur and professional photographers.

The Zeiss Ikon Contessa is a compact and stylish 35mm rangefinder camera produced by Zeiss Ikon from 1950 to 1971. It features a high-quality Zeiss Tessar lens with a maximum aperture of f/2.8, providing excellent image sharpness and clarity. The camera has a built-in coupled rangefinder, allowing for precise focusing and accurate composition. The Contessa offers a range of shutter speeds from 1/30 to 1/500 second, giving photographers the flexibility to capture a wide variety of subjects and lighting conditions. It also has a built-in light meter for easy exposure control. The Contessa is known for its solid build quality and reliable performance, making it a popular choice among photography enthusiasts and professionals.

The Ikoflex Ic (model 886/16) was a German twin-lens reflex camera manufactured by Zeiss Ikon from 1956 onwards, representing an evolution of the popular Ikoflex series. What distinguished this model from earlier Ikoflex cameras was the integration of a selenium exposure meter positioned on the front panel where the traditional nameplate had been located, with exposure readings visible at the top of the ground glass for convenient viewing. The camera was available with two lens configurations: either a coated Novar 3.5/75mm or the premium coated Tessar 3.5/75mm lens, both mounted in Prontor-SVS shutters, paired with a Teronar-Anastigmat f/3.5 viewing lens. Notable features included double-exposure prevention, blank frame prevention, M and X flash synchronization, a built-in self-timer, and a sports finder in the hood for quick action photography. The uncoupled light meter provided readings from LV 2 to 16, while an exposure value calculator on the focus knob accommodated film speeds from 5 to 320 ASA. Weighing approximately 1070 grams, the Ikoflex Ic offered advanced metering capabilities while maintaining the classic 6×6 format TLR design that made these cameras popular among both amateur and professional photographers.

The Zeiss Ikon Ikoflex IIa is a medium format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera produced by Zeiss Ikon in Germany, introduced around 1952. It uses 120 roll film to produce 6x6 cm square images. The camera features a Tessar 75mm f/3.5 taking lens and a matching viewing lens, with a Synchro-Compur shutter offering speeds from 1 second to 1/500 second plus Bulb mode. Focusing is achieved via a knob on the side, and the camera includes a waist-level viewfinder with a pop-up magnifier for critical focusing. The Ikoflex IIa is notable for its robust build quality and precise lens, making it popular among enthusiasts of classic TLRs. It also includes flash synchronization and self-timer functions.

The Zeiss Ikon Ikonta 521 is a medium format folding camera produced by Zeiss Ikon from 1936 to 1951. It features a high-quality 75mm f/3.5 Tessar lens, which produces sharp and detailed images. The camera has a sturdy metal body and a leatherette covering, giving it a classic and elegant look. It has a folding bellows design, allowing for compact storage when not in use. The Ikonta 521 has a range of shutter speeds from 1/25 to 1/250 seconds, as well as a bulb mode for long exposures. It uses 120 roll film, which allows for 8 exposures of 6x9cm or 12 exposures of 6x6cm. The camera has a built-in brilliant viewfinder for easy framing and composition. Overall, the Zeiss Ikonta 521 is a reliable and versatile medium format camera, suitable for both amateur and professional photographers.

The Zeiss Ikon Nettar is a medium format folding camera that was produced by Zeiss Ikon from 1934 to 1951. It is known for its compact and lightweight design, making it a popular choice for amateur photographers. The camera features a bellows system that allows for easy folding and unfolding, making it highly portable and convenient to carry. It uses 120 roll film, which provides high-resolution images with excellent detail. The Nettar is equipped with a high-quality Zeiss Ikon lens, known for its sharpness and clarity. It has a range of shutter speeds and aperture settings, allowing for versatile shooting in different lighting conditions. The camera also has a built-in viewfinder and a tripod mount for added stability. Overall, the Zeiss Ikon Nettar is a reliable and compact medium format camera that delivers excellent image quality.

The Zeiss Ikon ZM is a high-quality 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Zeiss Ikon in 2004. It is designed for photographers who appreciate the precision and craftsmanship of traditional film cameras. The ZM features a durable metal body with a classic design, reminiscent of the iconic Leica M cameras. It is compatible with Leica M-mount lenses, allowing photographers to take advantage of the excellent optics available in the Leica lens lineup. The camera has a bright and clear viewfinder with a built-in rangefinder for accurate focusing. It offers manual exposure control, allowing photographers to have full creative control over their images. The ZM also has a built-in light meter for convenient exposure metering. Overall, the Zeiss Ikon ZM is a reliable and versatile camera that combines the best of traditional craftsmanship with modern functionality.

The Super Ikonta 532/16 is a folding camera produced by the German company Zeiss Ikon from 1937 to 1955. It is part of the Ikonta line and takes 11 6x6 cm images on 120 type rollfilm. This model was an upgrade from its predecessor, the Super Ikonta 530/16, and was designed to resolve frame overlapping issues. It features a coupled rangefinder, with the rangefinder and viewfinder windows combined. The 532/16 was generally sold as the Super Ikonta I 6x6 cm or Super Ikonta I 2 1/4 x 2 1/4. It came equipped with an 8cm f2.8 Tessar lens in a Compur-Rapid shutter and included an automatic film stop and frame counting mechanism. Post-war models could also feature a Synchro-Compur shutter with X-synchronization and M-synchronization, and had a self-timer. The camera also included double exposure prevention and an accessory shoe for items like the Contameter and Albada finder.

The Zenit 12 is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera produced by KMZ in Russia from 1983 to 1994. It is an improved version of the earlier Zenit TTL, featuring updates for greater reliability and construction quality. The Zenit 12SD variant includes a restyled shutter speed dial, with later 12SD models featuring a redesigned top plate and pentaprism housing. The Zenit 12XP is closely related to the 12SD, but replaces the traditional meter needle with LED exposure indicators in the viewfinder. Additionally, a version of the Zenit 12XP was manufactured in Brazil by BMA INDÚSTRIA E COMÉRCIO LTDA. All models in the Zenit 12 series are known for their mechanical simplicity and use of the M42 lens mount.

The Zenit 122 is a Soviet-era 35mm SLR camera produced from 1990 to 2005 and features an M42 screw mount for interchangeable lenses. Constructed with a plastic body but retaining a solid, weighty feel, it offers fully manual operation with shutter speeds from Bulb to 1/500s and a mechanical self-timer. The camera includes a basic, battery-powered match LED light meter visible in the viewfinder, along with a split-image focusing screen for precise manual focus. The Zenit 122 is compatible with a wide range of M42 lenses and is often paired with the Helios 44M-7 58mm f/2 lens, known for its sharpness and character. While the build is utilitarian and the mirror slap is pronounced, it delivers reliable mechanical performance. The 122K variant uses a Pentax K mount instead, but otherwise shares the same features.

The Zenit E is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera manufactured by KMZ (Krasnogorsky Mekhanichesky Zavod) in the Soviet Union, first introduced in 1965. It uses standard 35mm film and features a M42 screw mount for interchangeable lenses. The camera is fully mechanical, with a shutter speed range from 1/30 to 1/500 second plus Bulb mode. Notably, the Zenit E includes a built-in, uncoupled selenium light meter, which does not require batteries. The viewfinder is a simple optical pentaprism type, and the camera lacks automatic exposure or focusing aids. Its robust, all-metal construction contributed to its popularity and longevity, with millions produced until 1986.

The Zenit TTL is a 35mm single-lens reflex (SLR) camera manufactured by KMZ (Krasnogorsky Mekhanichesky Zavod) in the Soviet Union, first introduced in 1977. It uses the M42 screw mount for interchangeable lenses and features a built-in through-the-lens (TTL) CdS exposure meter. The camera offers manual exposure control with shutter speeds ranging from 1/30 to 1/500 second plus Bulb mode. Focusing is manual, and the viewfinder provides a central microprism spot for easier focusing. The Zenit TTL is fully mechanical, requiring a battery only for the light meter. Its robust metal construction and simple operation made it popular among amateur photographers.

The Zorki 4 is a popular 35mm rangefinder camera that was introduced by Zorki in 1956. It is a fully manual camera, and does not have a lightmeter. An additional lightmeter may be added by the cold shoe. The early bodies have a vulcanite body covering, engraved shutter speeds, and strap lugs. As with other Soviet-era rangefinders, the shutter speed selector rotates when the shutter is released, and should not be changed until after the shutter has been cocked.

The Plaubel Makina 67 is a 6x7 strut folding camera with a coupled rangefinder, released in March 1979. It was developed by Plaubel after the company was acquired by the Japanese company Doi in 1975. The camera features a lens designed by Nikon and its exterior design was influenced by professor Udo M. Geissler and lead designer Yasuo Uchida. It has a Nikkor 80mm f/2.8 lens.

The Pentacon Six mount, also known as P6 or Б in Cyrillic, is a medium format lens mount that was likely introduced by KW in collaboration with Carl Zeiss Jena. It is characterized by an external bayonet coupling. This mount is utilized across a variety of cameras, including the Praktisix, Pentacon Six, Exakta 66, Kiev 6C, Kiev 60, Kiev 88CM, Hartblei, and Arax. Lenses for this mount were produced by manufacturers such as Schneider in West Germany, Carl Zeiss Jena in East Germany, and the Arsenal factory in Kiev, Ukraine. The Arsenal factory continues to produce lenses for this mount, with its Arsat 30mm fisheye being particularly recognized for its quality. Hartblei in the Czech Republic and Arax in Ukraine also update and refine these lenses, notably producing a range of tilt-shift lenses with independently rotatable tilt and shift axes.

The Tachihara 4x5 is a traditional field camera produced by Tachihara Camera Works, a Japanese manufacturer based in Kita-ku, Tokyo, until at least 2013. These cameras are known for their moderate price and high quality, offering extensive lens board and image plane movements. They were available in various sizes, including 4x5, and came in cherry wood finishes (natural or 'rose-mahogany' varnished) or black-painted, with brass fittings in gold-color or chrome. Models included double- and triple-extension options, as well as a 'super-wide' version with short extension and bellows. The most common model, the Fiel Stand 45, sometimes featured a rear-focus mechanism, allowing the rear standard to move forward for close-up focusing or to accommodate wide-angle lenses without the bed appearing in the view. Tachihara cameras were also sold by Zone VI.

The Gowlandflex is a large-format twin-lens reflex (TLR) camera, most notably the 4x5 Glamour Camera, designed by California photographer Peter Gowland. Gowland, known for his glamour and celebrity photography, created the Gowlandflex to combine the mobility and continuous viewing of 6x6cm TLRs with the 4x5-inch negative format preferred for magazine-cover and pinup work. Constructed in Gowland's home workshop from lightweight aluminum, the 8-pound camera was designed to be handheld. Later models incorporated a ramp-shaped cam to correct parallax error by raising and lowering the viewing lensboard. Gowland claimed to have sold 1,500 cameras across his designs, with 600 being the popular 4x5 TLR model. Other variants included an 8x10 version and a Wide Angle Gowlandflex.

The Nishika 3-D N8000 is a variant of the Nimslo 3D, manufactured by the USA company Nishika in 1989. This camera is equipped with four 30mm lenses, designed to produce negatives on 35mm film. These negatives are intended for creating autostereoscopic prints.

The Seagull 4A is a 6x6 TLR camera for 120 roll film, manufactured in Shanghai, China, by the Shanghai Camera Factory. Introduced in the late 1960s as a complement to the 1964 Seagull 4, it is known to have been in production for at least 40 years. This camera features a right-hand wind-on crank with an automatic frame counter and is considered a Rolleiflex copy, though it has 34mm filter threads. It includes a fixed finder hood with a built-in action finder and a critical focusing magnifier. The taking optic is a HAIOU-31 SA 1:3.5/75 coated lens, while the finder optic is a nameless 1:2.8/75 lens. A depth-of-field scale is integrated into the focusing knob. The five-bladed, fully synchronized leaf shutter offers speeds from B to 1/300 second. The camera also includes a PC sync contact, a threaded release button, and a self-timer lever.

The Widelux F7 is a swing-lens panorama camera manufactured by Panon Camera Shoko in Tokyo between 1979 and 1988. It is part of the Widelux F-series, which uses 35mm film and provides a horizontal coverage of approximately 126° and a vertical coverage of 55°, resulting in a 24 x 59mm image size. The camera operates on a principle where a lens swivels through a horizontal arc, projecting an image onto a cylindrical film gate. This design is similar to other panoramic cameras like the Noblex and Horizont. The Widelux F7 is known for producing characteristic banding in images due to uneven movement of the lens turret, often caused by dust and grime in the gears. Approximately 20,000 total 35mm Widelux cameras were produced across all F-series models.

The Revue ML is a 35mm SLR camera, also known as the Praktica MTL 5 B, manufactured by Pentacon in Dresden, East Germany, between 1985 and 1989. It features TTL exposure metering, activated by a stop-down button, with a match-needle display in the viewfinder indicating exposure levels. The camera's meter is powered by a battery, which was a PX25 mercury battery in early models and an LR44 alkaline battery in later versions, though metering is optional. Film speed is set via the shutter speed dial. It is equipped with a metal-curtained focal plane shutter offering speeds from 1s to 1/1000s, plus Bulb mode, and includes a self-timer. Flash synchronization is available at 1/125 second. The Revue ML uses interchangeable M42 screw mount lenses, commonly found with the Meyer-designed Pentacon auto 1.8/50mm multi-coated lens. The viewfinder incorporates a split-prism/microprism focusing aid with a diagonal split.

The Agfa Isolette III is a compact horizontal-folding camera produced by Agfa Kamerawerk AG from 1952 to 1958. It is notable for being the best-specified Isolette model, featuring an uncoupled rangefinder operated by a thumb-wheel. The camera uses 120 film for twelve 6x6 cm pictures and has front-element focusing. It was equipped with either an 85mm f/4.5 Apotar lens with a Pronto or Prontor SV/SVS shutter, or an 85mm f/4.5 Solinar lens with a Synchro-Compur shutter, or a 75mm f/3.5 Solinar lens with a Prontor SVS or Synchro-Compur (MX/MXV) shutter. Some later models included a film reminder dial. It was also sold in the USA as the Ansco Speedex Special R.

The Sinar P is a 4x5 monorail view camera introduced in 1970 by Sinar. It is part of the Sinar camera line, which began with the original Sinar model, patented in 1947. Carl Hans Koch launched the fully modular Sinar system in 1948.

The LOMO Smena 8m is an entry-level 35mm camera from the 1970s Soviet Union. It is a fully manual camera with a plastic body. The Smena 8m features a 40mm f/4 T-43 Triplet coated glass lens, which provides contrast and saturation. It has a leaf shutter and a PC sync socket, allowing for flash synchronization at any shutter speed. Focus is set by estimating the distance to the subject and adjusting the lens accordingly. The shutter release requires manual cocking before each shot. The Smena 8m is known for being one of the most produced 35mm film cameras, with over 21 million units produced between 1963 and 1995, including its predecessor, the Smena 8.
